1-chronicles-1:1:1.summary: Luke’s genealogy ends with “Enosh, of Seth, of Adam,” the same first three names listed here.
1-chronicles-1:1:1.why: Shows Luke tracing Jesus back through this line.

1-chronicles-1:1:2.summary: Sirach praises “Seth” and “Adam” by name, the first figures in this genealogy.
1-chronicles-1:1:2.why: Shows later honor given to these first ancestors.

1-chronicles-1:2:0.summary: Luke’s genealogy lists “Jared, of Mahalalel, of Cainan,” the same three ancestors as Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared.
1-chronicles-1:2:0.why: Places this line in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:2:2.summary: Genesis records Enosh begetting “Cainan,” the Kenan who opens this verse.
1-chronicles-1:2:2.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:3:3.summary: Luke’s list includes “Lamech,” “Methuselah,” and “Enoch,” the same three ancestors.
1-chronicles-1:3:3.why: Places this line in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:3:0.summary: Jude names “Enoch,” “the seventh from Adam,” the Enoch of this list.
1-chronicles-1:3:0.why: Shows Enoch remembered as a prophet.

1-chronicles-1:3:2.summary: Hebrews tells how “Enoch was taken away” by faith, the same Enoch listed here.
1-chronicles-1:3:2.why: Gives Enoch’s story behind the bare name.

1-chronicles-1:4:1.summary: Genesis names “the sons of Noah… Shem, Ham, and Japheth,” the same three sons.
1-chronicles-1:4:1.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:4:8.summary: Genesis says “Noah begot three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth,” matching this verse.
1-chronicles-1:4:8.why: Gives the Genesis source and Noah’s righteousness.

1-chronicles-1:4:2.summary: God calls Noah, the same Noah listed here, righteous and tells him to enter the ark.
1-chronicles-1:4:2.why: Supplies Noah’s story behind the name.

1-chronicles-1:4:3.summary: Genesis gives the full lifespan and death of Noah, the same patriarch listed.

1-chronicles-1:4:4.summary: Luke’s genealogy runs “of Shem, of Noah,” the same father and son named here.
1-chronicles-1:4:4.why: Places Noah and Shem in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:4:5.summary: Jesus uses “the days of Noah” as a picture of His coming; only the name is shared.
1-chronicles-1:4:5.why: Shows Noah’s era used as a warning.

1-chronicles-1:4:6.summary: Ezekiel names “Noah” as a model righteous man, the same patriarch listed here.
1-chronicles-1:4:6.why: Shows Noah’s later reputation for righteousness.

1-chronicles-1:4:7.summary: Peter says God “preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness,” the same Noah.
1-chronicles-1:4:7.why: Shows Noah’s role in the flood story.

1-chronicles-1:4:9.summary: Hebrews praises “Noah” for building the ark by faith, the same patriarch.
1-chronicles-1:4:9.why: Shows Noah as an example of faith.

1-chronicles-1:4:10.summary: Isaiah recalls God’s oath in “Noah’s time”; Noah is only a time marker.
1-chronicles-1:4:10.why: Links Noah to God’s covenant promise.

1-chronicles-1:4:11.summary: Jesus compares His coming to “the days of Noah”; only the name connects.
1-chronicles-1:4:11.why: Shows Noah’s era used as a warning.

1-chronicles-1:5:1.summary: Ezekiel names “Gomer” among Gog’s allies, the same people as Japheth’s son Gomer.

1-chronicles-1:5:2.summary: Ezekiel’s “Greece” stands for Javan, but the Saints wording does not show the name Javan.
1-chronicles-1:5:2.why: Link depends on Javan being Greece.

1-chronicles-1:5:3.summary: Ezekiel names “Magog” along with “Mosoch and Thobel,” which match Magog, Meshech, and Tubal here.
1-chronicles-1:5:3.why: Traces Japheth’s peoples into the Gog prophecy.

1-chronicles-1:5:4.summary: Ezekiel names “Mosoch and Thobel,” the Greek forms of Meshech and Tubal, but not Magog.
1-chronicles-1:5:4.why: Link depends on matching variant name forms.

1-chronicles-1:7:0.summary: Balaam’s oracle mentions “the Kitians,” the same people listed among Javan’s sons.

1-chronicles-1:7:1.summary: Isaiah names “Tharsis” and “Greece” among the nations, matching Tharsis and Javan’s line.
1-chronicles-1:7:1.why: Shows these peoples receiving God’s glory.

1-chronicles-1:7:2.summary: Isaiah names “the Kitians” as a refuge for Sidon, the same people listed here.

1-chronicles-1:7:3.summary: The psalm names “kings of Tarshish,” the Tharsis listed among Javan’s sons.
1-chronicles-1:7:3.why: Shows this distant people bringing gifts.

1-chronicles-1:7:4.summary: The Saints text reads “Romans,” not Kitians, so the shared name does not appear.
1-chronicles-1:7:4.why: Link relies on wording absent here.

1-chronicles-1:7:5.summary: Jeremiah names “the islands of Kittim,” the Kitians listed among Javan’s sons.

1-chronicles-1:7:6.summary: Isaiah mentions “the Kitians’ land,” the same people listed here.

1-chronicles-1:7:7.summary: Ezekiel mentions “the islands of Kittim,” the Kitians of this list.
1-chronicles-1:7:7.why: Shows this people in Tyre’s trade.

1-chronicles-1:10:1.summary: Micah names “Nebrod’s land,” the land of Nimrod named in this verse.
1-chronicles-1:10:1.why: Shows Nimrod’s land in later prophecy.

1-chronicles-1:17:1.summary: Balaam’s oracle mentions “Asshur” and “Assyrians,” the people of Shem’s son Asshur.

1-chronicles-1:17:2.summary: Ezekiel lists Persians, Lydians, and Libyans; none of Elam, Asshur, or Arphaxad appear.
1-chronicles-1:17:2.why: No shared name in the shown text.

1-chronicles-1:17:3.summary: Isaiah names “the Assyrians” and “the Elamites,” peoples descended from Shem’s sons Asshur and Elam.
1-chronicles-1:17:3.why: Shows these peoples in the promised regathering.

1-chronicles-1:17:4.summary: Isaiah’s list names Tharsis, Phoud, Loud, and others, but not Elam, Asshur, or Arphaxad.
1-chronicles-1:17:4.why: No shared name in the shown text.

1-chronicles-1:17:5.summary: Jeremiah names “all Elam’s kings,” the people of Shem’s son Elam.

1-chronicles-1:17:6.summary: Isaiah describes “the Elamites” as warriors, descendants of Shem’s son Elam.

1-chronicles-1:17:7.summary: Genesis records that Shem “begot Arphaxad,” the same son named here.
1-chronicles-1:17:7.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:17:8.summary: Ezekiel’s lament places “Assyria” in the pit, the people of Asshur named here.
1-chronicles-1:17:8.why: Traces Asshur’s people to their judgment.

1-chronicles-1:17:9.summary: Chedorlaomer is “king of Elam,” but Elam is only mentioned in passing.
1-chronicles-1:17:9.why: Shows Elam as an early kingdom.

1-chronicles-1:17:10.summary: “Asshur” appears in a list of Tyre’s traders, a passing mention.
1-chronicles-1:17:10.why: Shows Asshur as a trading nation.

1-chronicles-1:17:11.summary: Ezekiel’s lament describes “Elam and all his force” in the pit, the nation from Shem’s son Elam.

1-chronicles-1:17:12.summary: The psalm lists “Asshur” among Israel’s enemies, a passing mention.

1-chronicles-1:17:13.summary: Israel says “Assur will certainly not save us,” naming the nation but nothing about its ancestry.
1-chronicles-1:17:13.why: Shows Assyria as a false hope.

1-chronicles-1:17:14.summary: Balaam comes “from Mesopotamia”; none of the names in this verse appear.
1-chronicles-1:17:14.why: No shared name in the shown text.

1-chronicles-1:17:15.summary: “The Elamites” appear in Isaiah’s vision, a passing mention.
1-chronicles-1:17:15.why: Shows Elam in a later oracle.

1-chronicles-1:17:16.summary: “Assour” appears only in a king’s title, a passing mention.

1-chronicles-1:17:17.summary: “Elymais” and “Ailam” reflect Elam, but only as Daniel’s location.

1-chronicles-1:24:0.summary: The Genesis genealogy from Shem runs through Arphaxad and Cainan to “Shelah,” the Sala of this verse.
1-chronicles-1:24:0.why: Gives the Genesis source; the range is truncated.

1-chronicles-1:24:1.summary: Luke’s genealogy includes “Shelah” with Arphaxad and Cainan, matching Sala’s place in this line.
1-chronicles-1:24:1.why: Places this line in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:25:0.summary: Luke’s genealogy runs “of Reu, of Peleg, of Eber,” matching Eber, Peleg, Ragau.
1-chronicles-1:25:0.why: Places this line in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:26:0.summary: Luke lists “Terah, of Nahor, of Serug,” the same three ancestors.
1-chronicles-1:26:0.why: Places this line in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:27:0.summary: Nehemiah recalls God choosing Abram and naming him “Abraam.”
1-chronicles-1:27:0.why: Explains Abraham’s calling and new name.

1-chronicles-1:27:1.summary: Genesis records “Terah begot Abram,” continuing the same line to Abraham.
1-chronicles-1:27:1.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:27:2.summary: Joshua names “Terah, the father of Abraham,” the same line.
1-chronicles-1:27:2.why: Adds Terah’s worship of other gods.

1-chronicles-1:28:0.summary: The angel announces Ishmael’s birth and name, the son of Abraham listed here.
1-chronicles-1:28:0.why: Gives the story of Ishmael’s birth.

1-chronicles-1:28:1.summary: Sarah sees Hagar’s son with “Isaac her son,” the two sons of Abraham named here.
1-chronicles-1:28:1.why: Shows the tension between the two sons.

1-chronicles-1:28:2.summary: God tells Abraham that “in Isaac seed shall be called to you,” contrasting the slave woman’s child.
1-chronicles-1:28:2.why: Explains why Isaac carries the promise.

1-chronicles-1:28:3.summary: Genesis tells the birth of Abraham’s son “Isaac,” named first in this verse.
1-chronicles-1:28:3.why: Gives the story of Isaac’s birth.

1-chronicles-1:28:4.summary: God promises a covenant with “Isaac” and a blessing on “Ishmael,” the two sons listed.
1-chronicles-1:28:4.why: Explains the different futures of the two sons.

1-chronicles-1:29:1.summary: The Saints verse speaks of arrows and “desert coals” and does not name Kedar or Ishmael.
1-chronicles-1:29:1.why: Link relies on a neighboring verse.

1-chronicles-1:29:2.summary: Isaiah foretells the decline of “Kedar’s strong sons,” the tribe from Ishmael’s son Kedar.

1-chronicles-1:29:3.summary: Esau marries a daughter of Ishmael, “the sister of Nebaioth,” the Nabaioth listed here.

1-chronicles-1:29:4.summary: The bride compares herself to “the tents of Kedar,” a passing image.

1-chronicles-1:29:5.summary: Isaiah names “Kedar’s sheep” and “Nabaioth’s rams,” the first two of Ishmael’s sons.
1-chronicles-1:29:5.why: Shows these tribes joining God’s worship.

1-chronicles-1:30:1.summary: “Idumea” in Isaiah may reflect Dumah, the Idouma here, but the forms differ.
1-chronicles-1:30:1.why: Link depends on matching variant names.

1-chronicles-1:32:1.summary: The “elders of Midian” appear in the Balaam story; Midian is only named.
1-chronicles-1:32:1.why: Shows Midian’s later role against Israel.

1-chronicles-1:32:2.summary: Moses is told to take vengeance “from the Midianites,” descendants of Keturah’s son Midian.
1-chronicles-1:32:2.why: Shows Midian as Israel’s later enemy.

1-chronicles-1:32:3.summary: The Saints text reads “Arabia’s gold,” not Saba, so no listed name appears.
1-chronicles-1:32:3.why: Link relies on wording absent here.

1-chronicles-1:32:4.summary: Midian oppresses Israel in Gideon’s day, a people named after Keturah’s son Midian.
1-chronicles-1:32:4.why: Shows Midian as Israel’s later enemy.

1-chronicles-1:32:5.summary: Jeremiah’s oracle addresses the “inhabitants of Dedan,” the Daidan of this list.

1-chronicles-1:32:6.summary: “Dedan” appears as Tyre’s trader, the same people as Daidan here.

1-chronicles-1:32:7.summary: Moses flees to “the land of Midian”; Midian is a setting only.

1-chronicles-1:32:8.summary: The queen of Sheba may come from Saba’s line, but the names differ in form.
1-chronicles-1:32:8.why: Link depends on Sheba being Saba.

1-chronicles-1:32:9.summary: Ezekiel names Idumea and Thaiman, neither of which is in this verse.
1-chronicles-1:32:9.why: No shared name in the shown text.

1-chronicles-1:32:10.summary: Isaiah names “Madiam,” “Gaipha,” and “Saba,” matching Midian, Ephah, and Saba of Keturah’s line.
1-chronicles-1:32:10.why: Shows these peoples bringing gifts to Zion.

1-chronicles-1:32:11.summary: Isaiah’s oracle mentions “Daidan’s road,” the Daidan named here.

1-chronicles-1:32:12.summary: The psalm lists “Saba” among kings bringing gifts, a passing mention.
1-chronicles-1:32:12.why: Shows Saba as a distant gift-bearer.

1-chronicles-1:32:13.summary: “The Sabeans” may descend from Saba, but the link is only a trade route.

1-chronicles-1:32:14.summary: “Midianite merchants” sell Joseph; Midian is only named in passing.

1-chronicles-1:32:15.summary: “Dedan” appears in Jeremiah’s list of judged peoples, a passing mention.

1-chronicles-1:32:16.summary: A “Midianite woman” appears at Peor, a passing mention.
1-chronicles-1:32:16.why: Shows Midian’s later conflict with Israel.

1-chronicles-1:33:0.summary: Isaiah names “Madiam and Gaipha,” matching Midian and his son Gaipha in this verse.
1-chronicles-1:33:0.why: Shows Midian’s line bringing gifts to Zion.

1-chronicles-1:34:2.summary: Matthew opens with “Abraham begot Isaac; and Isaac begot Jacob,” the same line.
1-chronicles-1:34:2.why: Places this line in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:34:0.summary: Jacob, Isaac’s son, is renamed “Israel,” the name Chronicles often uses for him.

1-chronicles-1:34:1.summary: Genesis tells the birth of Abraham’s son “Isaac,” named in this verse.
1-chronicles-1:34:1.why: Gives the story of Isaac’s birth.

1-chronicles-1:34:3.summary: Stephen says “Abraham fathered Isaac… Isaac fathered Jacob,” the same line.
1-chronicles-1:34:3.why: Shows the line retold in Acts.

1-chronicles-1:34:4.summary: Luke lists “Jacob, of Isaac, of Abraham,” the same three generations.
1-chronicles-1:34:4.why: Places this line in Jesus’ genealogy.

1-chronicles-1:34:5.summary: Paul discusses Isaac’s twin sons, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
1-chronicles-1:34:5.why: Shows the theological meaning of the two brothers.

1-chronicles-1:34:7.summary: Malachi names “Esau Jacob’s brother,” the two sons of Isaac listed here.
1-chronicles-1:34:7.why: Shows the later histories of the two brothers.

1-chronicles-1:34:8.summary: The earlier verse names “Abraham’s sons: Isaac and Ishmael,” leading into this verse.

1-chronicles-1:35:1.summary: Genesis lists Esau’s sons, including “Eliphaz” and “Reuel,” matching Eliphaz and Ragouel.
1-chronicles-1:35:1.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:36:0.summary: Amos’s oracle on “Teman” names the Edomite region linked to Eliphaz’s son Teman.

1-chronicles-1:36:1.summary: Jeremiah judges “Teman’s inhabitants,” the region linked to Eliphaz’s son Teman.

1-chronicles-1:36:2.summary: Jeremiah laments that “there is no longer wisdom in Teman,” the region named for Teman.

1-chronicles-1:36:4.summary: The later list names “Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman,” matching two of Eliphaz’s sons.
1-chronicles-1:36:4.why: Shows these names as Edomite chiefs.

1-chronicles-1:36:5.summary: Obadiah threatens the “warriors from Teman,” the region named for Teman.

1-chronicles-1:36:6.summary: “Teman” is the region God comes from; it is only a place name.

1-chronicles-1:39:0.summary: The “Horites” of Seir may connect to Chorri, but the forms differ.
1-chronicles-1:39:0.why: Link depends on Chorri being Hori.

1-chronicles-1:39:2.summary: The Horites are driven out of Seir; the link to Chorri rests on the name only.
1-chronicles-1:39:2.why: Link depends on Chorri being Hori.

1-chronicles-1:40:0.summary: Genesis lists “Shobal’s sons” and “Zibeon’s sons” with the same names in different spellings.
1-chronicles-1:40:0.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:41:0.summary: Genesis lists Anah’s son Dishon and his sons “Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran,” matching this verse.
1-chronicles-1:41:0.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:42:1.summary: Genesis lists Asar’s sons “Balaan, Zoukam” and Uz and Aram, matching this verse.
1-chronicles-1:42:1.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-1:42:0.summary: The Saints text addresses Idumea “dwelling upon the land” and does not name Uz.
1-chronicles-1:42:0.why: Link relies on wording absent here.

1-chronicles-1:43:1.summary: Jacob’s blessing on Judah does not mention Balak, Beor, Dennaba, or Edom’s kings.
1-chronicles-1:43:1.why: No shared name in the shown text.

1-chronicles-1:43:2.summary: Balaam foretells that “Edom shall become an inheritance,” but this verse does not name Edom.
1-chronicles-1:43:2.why: Shows Israel’s later rule over Edom.

1-chronicles-1:44:0.summary: Isaiah names “Bosor” in Idumea, the Bosorra from which Jobab came.

1-chronicles-1:44:1.summary: Isaiah’s figure comes “from Bosor” in Edom, the same city as Bosorra.

1-chronicles-1:44:2.summary: The Saints text does not name Bosor or Edom; it speaks only of “her midst.”
1-chronicles-1:44:2.why: Link relies on wording absent here.

1-chronicles-1:44:3.summary: Micah speaks of sheep “in affliction”; no Edomite place or king is named.
1-chronicles-1:44:3.why: Link relies on wording absent here.

1-chronicles-1:44:4.summary: Amos names Teman, not Bosorra, Jobab, or Zara.
1-chronicles-1:44:4.why: No shared name in the shown text.

1-chronicles-1:45:0.summary: Genesis names Eliphaz’s son “Teman,” the ancestor of the “Thaimans,” but no king.

1-chronicles-1:45:1.summary: Eliphaz is “king of the Temanites,” the people from the land of the Thaimans.
1-chronicles-1:45:1.why: Links Job’s friend to this region.

1-chronicles-1:47:0.summary: Genesis records “Hadad died, and Samlah from Masrekah reigned,” the same succession.
1-chronicles-1:47:0.why: Gives the Genesis source of the king list.

1-chronicles-1:48:0.summary: Genesis records “Shaul from Rehoboth by the River” succeeding Samlah, the same succession.
1-chronicles-1:48:0.why: Gives the Genesis source of the king list.

1-chronicles-1:51:0.summary: Genesis lists Esau’s chiefs “Timna,” “Gola,” and “Jether,” matching this list.
1-chronicles-1:51:0.why: Gives the Genesis source of the list.

1-chronicles-2:1:1.summary: Lists the tribes Judah, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun among the sealed, a later and altered tribal list.
1-chronicles-2:1:1.why: Echo of Israel’s sons in Revelation.

1-chronicles-2:1:6.summary: Lists Israel’s sons in the same order: “Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah; Issachar, Zebulun.”

1-chronicles-2:1:0.summary: Explains Jacob’s new name “Israel,” the father named in the source list.

1-chronicles-2:1:3.summary: “These are the names of the sons of Israel,” beginning with Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun (truncated).

1-chronicles-2:1:4.summary: Jacob’s blessings address Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah and the other sons in sequence (truncated).

1-chronicles-2:1:5.summary: Calls the “sons of Jacob” to hear “Israel your father,” only introducing the same sons.

1-chronicles-2:1:7.summary: Records Benjamin’s naming; he is one of Israel’s sons, though not in the shown source verse.
1-chronicles-2:1:7.why: Birth of one of the twelve.

1-chronicles-2:1:8.summary: A tribe-by-tribe list of spies (Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Issachar…) loosely follows the sons of Israel.

1-chronicles-2:1:9.summary: The census starts “Reuben was Israel’s firstborn” and proceeds tribe by tribe (truncated).

1-chronicles-2:1:10.summary: Narrates the births and naming of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, the first sons listed.
1-chronicles-2:1:10.why: Origins of the first four sons.

1-chronicles-2:1:11.summary: Tribal leaders listed for Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun; a related tribal list.

1-chronicles-2:1:12.summary: Narrates the births of Dan, Naphtali and other sons of Israel named in the list (truncated).

1-chronicles-2:3:1.summary: “The sons of Judah were Er and Onan … died,” paralleling Er and Onan’s listing and death.

1-chronicles-2:3:2.summary: “Judah’s sons: Er, Onan, Shelah …. But Er and Onan died,” matching the source.

1-chronicles-2:3:3.summary: The “Selonites” are descendants of Shelon, Judah’s son named here.

1-chronicles-2:4:0.summary: “Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar” parallels Tamar bearing Phares and Zara.

1-chronicles-2:4:2.summary: Begins “the generations of Perez,” the Phares born to Judah by Tamar.

1-chronicles-2:4:3.summary: Mentions “the sons of Phares” among Judah’s returnees, descendants of this Phares.

1-chronicles-2:4:4.summary: “Zara’s sons” among returnees descend from the Zara named here.

1-chronicles-2:4:5.summary: Judah’s clans from Shelon, Perez, and Zerah parallel Judah’s five sons.
1-chronicles-2:4:5.why: Clan list from the same sons.

1-chronicles-2:4:6.summary: The Saints text names Pathaia son of Baseza without mentioning Zara or Phares.
1-chronicles-2:4:6.why: No shared name in the displayed text.

1-chronicles-2:4:7.summary: Calls Tamar Judah’s “daughter-in-law,” the same relationship named in the source.

1-chronicles-2:4:8.summary: Traces Gothi to “Phares son of Judah,” the Phares of this verse.

1-chronicles-2:4:9.summary: “Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah” restates the source’s birth notice.

1-chronicles-2:4:10.summary: This Zerah stands beside Shaul in a clan list apart from Judah’s, so it is not Judah’s son Zara.

1-chronicles-2:4:11.summary: Luke’s line “of Hezron, of Perez, of Judah” includes Perez, son of Judah.

1-chronicles-2:5:0.summary: “Perez’s sons were Hezron and Jemuel” parallels “Arson and Jemouel.”

1-chronicles-2:5:1.summary: “Perez begot Hezron” matches Phares’s son Arson.

1-chronicles-2:5:2.summary: “The sons of Perez: … Hezron … Iamun” parallels Arson and Jemouel.

1-chronicles-2:5:3.summary: Luke’s “of Hezron, of Perez” includes Phares and his son Arson.

1-chronicles-2:5:4.summary: “Perez begot Hezron” parallels Phares’s son Arson.

1-chronicles-2:6:0.summary: Solomon is wiser than “Gaithan … Heman, Calcol, and Darda,” matching Zara’s sons Ethan, Heman, Chalchal, Dara.
1-chronicles-2:6:0.why: Shows these men’s fame for wisdom.

1-chronicles-2:6:1.summary: “Achar son of Zambri, son of Zerah” connects to Zara’s son Zimri.

1-chronicles-2:6:2.summary: “Achar son of Carmi, son of Zambri, son of Zerah” links Zara’s son Zimri to the Achar story.

1-chronicles-2:7:0.summary: Warning not to take what is “under the ban” lest the camp be brought to ruin — the command Achar broke.

1-chronicles-2:7:1.summary: “They stole from what was under the ban,” the Lord’s account of Achar’s trespass (truncated).

1-chronicles-4:33:0.summary: Villages “around their cities as far as Barek” parallels farmsteads “as far as Baal”, closing Simeon's inheritance.

1-chronicles-4:38:0.summary: Rulers of ancestral houses in another tribe parallel the formula only generally.

1-chronicles-4:38:1.summary: Giants as “men of renown” share nothing with Simeonite rulers multiplying in the Saints wording.

1-chronicles-4:39:0.summary: “Geddon” does not match “Gerara” in the Saints text, so the assumed place link fails.

1-chronicles-4:39:1.summary: Gedor in the earlier genealogy does not match “Gerara” in the Saints text.

1-chronicles-4:39:2.summary: Gedor's father in the earlier genealogy does not match “Gerara” in the Saints text.

1-chronicles-4:39:3.summary: The king of Geder is unrelated to “Gerara” in the Saints text.

1-chronicles-4:40:0.summary: Danites find a quiet, secure people in a good land to take, paralleling Simeon's discovery of peaceful pasture; shown text only.
1-chronicles-4:40:0.why: Similar tribal migration to quiet land.

1-chronicles-4:40:1.summary: Ham and the curse on Canaan give background on the Hamite former inhabitants; shown text only.

1-chronicles-4:40:2.summary: “The sons of Ham” are listed, identifying the people who formerly dwelt there.

1-chronicles-4:40:3.summary: “The land of Ham” refers to Egypt, connected only by the name Ham.
1-chronicles-4:40:3.why: Shows another use of Ham's name.

1-chronicles-4:40:4.summary: “Ham's tents” refers to Egypt, linked only by the name Ham.
1-chronicles-4:40:4.why: Shows another use of Ham's name.

1-chronicles-4:41:0.summary: God setting the boundaries of nations is too general to link to this Simeonite conquest.

1-chronicles-4:41:1.summary: In Hezekiah's days he struck the foreigners, the same reign in which the Simeonites struck these peoples; shown text only.
1-chronicles-4:41:1.why: Places the raid in Hezekiah's era.

1-chronicles-4:41:2.summary: An oracle against the foreigners shares nothing specific with the Simeonite raid; shown text only.

1-chronicles-4:41:3.summary: The oracle against Idumea and Teman has no specific link to the Minaioi or Simeonite settlement.

1-chronicles-4:41:4.summary: The Saints text lists Sidonians, Midian, and Amalek, not the Minaioi, so the assumed name link fails.
1-chronicles-4:41:4.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-4:41:5.summary: Reuben and Gad seek land suited for their many livestock, paralleling settlement “because there were pastures for their livestock”.

1-chronicles-4:41:6.summary: The rulers “recorded by name” are those listed in this preceding passage.
1-chronicles-4:41:6.why: Identifies who carried out the raid.

1-chronicles-4:42:0.summary: Esau lived in the mountain of Seir, linked only by the place name.

1-chronicles-4:42:1.summary: Mentions the way of Mount Seir, linked only by the place name.

1-chronicles-4:43:0.summary: David strikes Amalek, but four hundred escape, explaining how a remnant of Amalek remained to be struck here.

1-chronicles-4:43:1.summary: Amalek appears among David's conquered peoples, linked only by the name Amalek.

1-chronicles-4:43:2.summary: Saul strikes Amalek, an earlier stage of the campaign whose remnant the Simeonites finish.

1-chronicles-4:43:3.summary: God vows to blot out Amalek's remembrance, the war the Simeonites carry forward against its remnant.
1-chronicles-4:43:3.why: Sets the divine mandate against Amalek.

1-chronicles-4:43:4.summary: Israel is commanded to blot out the name of Amalek, fulfilled in part by this defeat of its remnant.

1-chronicles-4:43:5.summary: The ark's carrying poles share only the formula “to this day”.

1-chronicles-4:43:6.summary: Luz built by a man from Bethel shares only the formula “to this day”.

1-chronicles-4:43:7.summary: The guards' false report shares only the phrase “until this very day”.

1-chronicles-4:43:8.summary: Judah's desolation “as on this day” shares only the formula.

1-chronicles-4:43:9.summary: The Field of Blood named “until today” shares only the formula.

1-chronicles-4:43:10.summary: Moses' unknown burial place shares only the formula “unto this day”.

1-chronicles-4:14:1.summary: Nehemiah 11:35 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
1-chronicles-4:14:1.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
1-chronicles-4:14:1.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

1-chronicles-4:30:0.summary: Nehemiah 11:28 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
1-chronicles-4:30:0.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
1-chronicles-4:30:0.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

1-chronicles-5:1:4.summary: Both open with “The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn,” the same genealogical heading for Reuben’s line.
1-chronicles-5:1:4.why: Shows the Chronicler drawing on the Exodus genealogy.

1-chronicles-5:1:0.summary: Genesis narrates Reuben lying with Bilhah, the act Chronicles cites as “went up upon his father’s bed.”
1-chronicles-5:1:0.why: Supplies the event behind Reuben’s loss of rights.

1-chronicles-5:1:1.summary: Jacob blesses Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh, the blessing Chronicles says passed to Joseph (shown text truncated).
1-chronicles-5:1:1.why: Shows how Joseph received the firstborn’s blessing.

1-chronicles-5:1:2.summary: Records the birth of Reuben as Leah’s first son, the basis of his status as firstborn.

1-chronicles-5:1:5.summary: Paul condemns a man having “his father’s wife,” the same kind of sin as Reuben’s, but no direct link.
1-chronicles-5:1:5.why: Shows the enduring gravity of this sin.

1-chronicles-5:1:6.summary: Osa’s son was made ruler though “not firstborn,” a loose parallel to firstborn rights passing elsewhere.

1-chronicles-5:1:7.summary: The law against lying with one’s “father’s wife” condemns Reuben’s type of offense, without naming him.

1-chronicles-5:1:8.summary: “The greater shall serve the lesser” reverses birth order, a general theme rather than Reuben’s case.
1-chronicles-5:1:8.why: Pattern of elder displaced by younger.

1-chronicles-5:1:9.summary: Prohibits uncovering “your father’s wife,” the general law Reuben’s act violated.

1-chronicles-5:1:10.summary: Lists Israel’s sons with Reuben first, a general genealogy rather than the birthright issue.
1-chronicles-5:1:10.why: Places Reuben at the head of the tribes.

1-chronicles-5:1:11.summary: Curses one who “lies with his father’s wife,” the type of sin Reuben committed.
1-chronicles-5:1:11.why: Covenant curse on Reuben’s kind of act.

1-chronicles-5:1:12.summary: “Jacob’s firstborn was Reuben” matches the Chronicler’s repeated statement that Reuben was firstborn.

1-chronicles-5:1:13.summary: Defines the firstborn’s right to a double portion, the “firstborn rights” Reuben forfeited to Joseph.

1-chronicles-5:1:14.summary: Caleb’s approach to Joshua at Gilgal has no connection to Reuben or the birthright.

1-chronicles-5:1:15.summary: “Reuben was Israel’s firstborn” in the census matches the Chronicler’s heading.

1-chronicles-5:1:16.summary: Mentions Reubenites (On son of Peleth, son of Reuben) in Korah’s revolt, unrelated to the birthright.

1-chronicles-5:1:17.summary: Names Reuben’s tribal leader Elizur in a census, only a general tribal mention.
1-chronicles-5:1:17.why: Reuben’s tribal standing in the wilderness.

1-chronicles-5:1:18.summary: Jesse’s older sons are passed over for David, a general theme of elder sons set aside.
1-chronicles-5:1:18.why: Illustrates God choosing beyond birth order.

1-chronicles-5:1:19.summary: Shares only the word “firstborn”; Christ as “firstborn of all creation” has no bearing on Reuben’s rights.

1-chronicles-5:2:0.summary: A “ruler” coming out of Judah echoes “from him came a leader,” applied to the Messiah.
1-chronicles-5:2:0.why: Shows Judah’s leadership fulfilled in Christ.

1-chronicles-5:2:1.summary: Micah foresees “a ruler” coming from Bethlehem among Judah’s thousands, matching the leader from Judah.

1-chronicles-5:2:2.summary: “Our Lord has sprung from Judah” is a general link to Judah’s pre-eminence, not the specific leader statement.

1-chronicles-5:2:4.summary: Pairs Ephraim/Manasseh with “Judah is My king,” reflecting Judah’s rule alongside Joseph’s tribes.
1-chronicles-5:2:4.why: Poetic echo of Judah ruling, Joseph strong.

1-chronicles-5:2:5.summary: Repeats “Judah is My king” beside Ephraim and Manasseh, mirroring Judah’s leadership and Joseph’s blessing.

1-chronicles-5:2:6.summary: A righteous king for David in whose days “Judah will be saved” is a broad royal-Judah theme.

1-chronicles-5:2:7.summary: God “chose Judah’s tribe” and David to shepherd Israel, explaining the leader who came from Judah.
1-chronicles-5:2:7.why: Shows the divine choice of Judah’s ruler.

1-chronicles-5:2:8.summary: Judah camps first with its ruler Nahshon, loosely reflecting Judah’s strength among the tribes.

1-chronicles-5:2:9.summary: Jesse’s seven sons are rejected before David, only indirectly related to Judah’s leader.

1-chronicles-5:2:10.summary: The anointing of David, the leader who arose from Judah as the Chronicler implies.

1-chronicles-5:2:11.summary: Jacob’s “blessing” rests “upon Joseph’s head,” matching “the blessing belonged to Joseph.”

1-chronicles-5:2:12.summary: Christ as “firstborn among many brothers” shares only a word with a verse about Judah and Joseph.

1-chronicles-5:2:13.summary: “Judah shall go up” first gives Judah a leading role, a loose echo of Judah’s strength.

1-chronicles-5:2:14.summary: “The Lion from the tribe of Judah” recalls Judah’s pre-eminence in general terms.

1-chronicles-5:2:15.summary: Caleb’s speech at Gilgal mentions Judah’s sons but nothing about Judah’s leadership or Joseph’s blessing.

1-chronicles-5:2:16.summary: Lists Leah’s sons, including Reuben as firstborn and Judah, only a general genealogy.

1-chronicles-5:2:17.summary: God sends Samuel to Jesse to find a king, background to David the leader from Judah.

1-chronicles-5:2:18.summary: Nahshon presents first as “ruler of the tribe of Judah,” a general sign of Judah’s precedence.

1-chronicles-5:2:19.summary: David reigning over all Israel loosely illustrates the leader who came from Judah.

1-chronicles-5:3:1.summary: Same list of Reuben’s sons (Hanoch/Enoch, Pallu/Phallous, Hezron/Arson, Carmi/Charmi) under the same heading.

1-chronicles-5:3:0.summary: Genesis gives the same four sons of Reuben, matching the Chronicler’s Greek name forms.

1-chronicles-5:3:2.summary: The census lists Reuben’s clans from the same four sons and traces Pallu’s line to Dathan and Abiram.

1-chronicles-5:6:1.summary: “Thaglath-phellasar king of Assour” is the same Assyrian king who deported Beera.

1-chronicles-5:6:2.summary: Thaglathphellasar takes Gilead and “deported them to the Assyrians,” the same deportation affecting the Reubenites.

1-chronicles-5:6:3.summary: Ahaz appeals to Thaglathphellasar, the same Assyrian king named in Beera’s deportation.

1-chronicles-5:7:0.summary: Both speak of the Reubenites’ “enrollment,” and 5:17 dates that same enrollment to Jotham and Jeroboam.

1-chronicles-5:8:0.summary: Baal-meon, built by Reuben’s sons, is the same town as Beelmaon where Bela dwelt.

1-chronicles-5:8:1.summary: Aroer appears in both as a town in the Transjordan settlement.

1-chronicles-5:8:2.summary: Both trace the same Reubenite line of Joel and Semei within the same genealogy.

1-chronicles-5:8:3.summary: The Greek-based text of Isaiah 17:2 has no mention of Aroer, so the assumed place link is absent.
1-chronicles-5:8:3.why: Wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-5:8:4.summary: “The house of Beelmon” in Reuben’s allotment is the same place as Beelmaon.

1-chronicles-5:8:5.summary: Mount Nebo in Moab shares the name of the town Nabau, but the mountain is not the settlement itself.

1-chronicles-5:8:6.summary: Moses ascends Mount Nebo; only the name links to the town Nabau.

1-chronicles-5:8:7.summary: “Nabau of Moab’s country” is the same place named in the Reubenite settlement.

1-chronicles-5:8:8.summary: The Greek-based text of Ezekiel 25:9 lacks Baal-meon, giving only Asimouth, so no shared place appears.
1-chronicles-5:8:8.why: Wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-5:9:0.summary: Reuben, Gad and Manasseh return with “very much livestock” to “the land of Gilead,” matching numerous livestock in Galaad.
1-chronicles-5:9:0.why: Shows the tribes’ pastoral wealth in Gilead.

1-chronicles-5:10:0.summary: The same Transjordan tribes war against the Hagarenes and seize “all their tents,” expanding the brief war notice.
1-chronicles-5:10:0.why: Fuller account of the same war.

1-chronicles-5:10:1.summary: The Greek-based source says “resident aliens,” not Hagrites, so the link to Hagar’s son Ishmael is absent.
1-chronicles-5:10:1.why: Wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-5:10:2.summary: Names “Hagarenes,” but the source reads “resident aliens,” so the assumed Hagrite link is missing in this text.
1-chronicles-5:10:2.why: Wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-5:10:3.summary: Hagar’s son playing with Isaac has no link to a source that reads “resident aliens.”
1-chronicles-5:10:3.why: No link in the Saints wording.

1-chronicles-5:11:0.summary: “All Bashan as far as Salcah” matches Gad living “in Basan as far as Selcha.”

1-chronicles-5:11:1.summary: Describes Gad’s inheritance in Gilead and Transjordan, the territory where Gad’s sons lived.

1-chronicles-5:11:2.summary: Gad builds Dibon, Aroer and other towns, but not Basan or Selcha.

1-chronicles-5:11:3.summary: “All Bashan, as far as Salcah” and its distribution to Reuben, Gad and Manasseh match the source’s region.

1-chronicles-5:16:0.summary: “Satrais the Sharonite” shares only the Sharon name, not the region the Gadites occupied.

1-chronicles-5:16:1.summary: The Greek-based Isaiah 35:2 mentions Jordan, Lebanon and Carmel, not Sharon, so the assumed place link is absent.
1-chronicles-5:16:1.why: Wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-5:16:2.summary: “A flower of the plain” lacks the name Sharon in this wording, so no place link remains.
1-chronicles-5:16:2.why: Wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-5:17:0.summary: Summarizes the reign of Jeroboam, the king of Israel in whose days the enrollment took place.

1-chronicles-5:17:1.summary: Records Jeroboam son of Joash becoming king, the Jeroboam named in the dating.

1-chronicles-5:17:2.summary: Records the accession of Jotham king of Judah, the Joatham of the enrollment date.
1-chronicles-5:17:2.why: Anchors the date in Judah’s history.

1-chronicles-5:17:3.summary: Jotham governs during Uzziah’s leprosy, the same Jotham named in the dating.

1-chronicles-5:17:4.summary: Records Jeroboam son of Joash reigning forty-one years, the king in whose days the enrollment occurred.

1-chronicles-5:17:5.summary: Introduces Jotham’s reign in Judah, the Joatham named in the enrollment date.

1-chronicles-5:18:0.summary: The sons of Reuben, Gad and half-Manasseh go out “equipped for battle,” about forty thousand, matching the source’s armed men.
1-chronicles-5:18:0.why: Earlier military role of the same tribes.

1-chronicles-5:18:1.summary: Registering those who “go out in Israel’s army” is a general military census theme.
1-chronicles-5:18:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-5:19:0.summary: Jettour and Naphes, Ishmael’s sons, are the ancestors of the Ituraeans and Naphisaeans fought here.

1-chronicles-5:19:1.summary: Jetur and Naphish among Ishmael’s sons correspond to the Ituraeans and Naphisaeans.

1-chronicles-5:19:2.summary: Both describe the Transjordan tribes’ war in the east, the same campaign told twice.
1-chronicles-5:19:2.why: Links the two notices of the war.

1-chronicles-5:20:0.summary: The fathers “hoped” and “cried out” and were rescued, echoing crying to God and hoping in Him in battle.
1-chronicles-5:20:0.why: Same pattern of trust and deliverance.

1-chronicles-5:20:1.summary: Those who “hope in Thee” are not abandoned, a general theme of hope.

1-chronicles-5:20:2.summary: Jehoshaphat “cried out” in battle and the Lord saved him, the same pattern of answered battle cry.

1-chronicles-5:20:3.summary: Trust in the Lord’s name over chariots gives victory, a general theme.

1-chronicles-5:20:4.summary: God “listened to a human being” and fought for Israel, echoing “He listened to them” in battle.
1-chronicles-5:20:4.why: Parallel of God hearing in war.

1-chronicles-5:20:5.summary: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, a general statement on trust.

1-chronicles-5:20:6.summary: Continues the same battle: many fell “for the war was from God.”
1-chronicles-5:20:6.why: Completes the account of the victory.

1-chronicles-5:20:7.summary: The Lord fought alongside Israel under Joshua, a general divine-warrior theme.

1-chronicles-5:20:8.summary: Blessing on the one “whose hope is in the Lord,” a general theme of hope.

1-chronicles-5:20:9.summary: Blessed is one who trusts in the Lord, a general hope theme without battle context.

1-chronicles-5:20:10.summary: Solomon asks God to hear Israel’s prayer when they “go out to war,” matching prayer answered in battle.
1-chronicles-5:20:10.why: Prayer in war heard by God.

1-chronicles-5:20:11.summary: “Blessed is the person who hopes in Thee” shares only the general hope theme.

1-chronicles-5:20:12.summary: Hezekiah and Isaiah “cried out to heaven” and the Lord destroyed the Assyrian army, the same answered-cry pattern.

1-chronicles-5:20:13.summary: Jehoshaphat “cried out” in battle, but this shown text does not record God’s response.

1-chronicles-5:20:14.summary: Saul seeking David on his bed has no link to crying to God in battle.

1-chronicles-5:20:15.summary: “Thus far the Lord has helped us” after battle is a general theme of divine help.

1-chronicles-5:20:16.summary: Israel “prevailed” while Moses raised his hands, a loose parallel of prevailing with divine aid.

1-chronicles-5:20:17.summary: Having “hoped beforehand in Christ” shares only the word hope.

1-chronicles-5:20:18.summary: Jehoshaphat’s plea “our eyes are upon Thee” before battle is a related theme, but no answer is shown.

1-chronicles-5:20:19.summary: Asa “cried to the Lord,” saying “we trust in Thee,” and the Lord struck the enemy, the same pattern.
1-chronicles-5:20:19.why: Close parallel of trust and victory.

1-chronicles-5:20:20.summary: God as “refuge and strength” in afflictions is a general trust theme.

1-chronicles-5:20:21.summary: Judah “cried to the Lord” in battle and the Lord struck Jeroboam, matching the answered battle cry.
1-chronicles-5:20:21.why: Parallel of crying out in war.

1-chronicles-5:21:0.summary: Revelation lists livestock and “human lives” as cargo, a verbal echo of “human lives” taken as plunder.
1-chronicles-5:21:0.why: Shared phrase for people as goods.

1-chronicles-5:21:1.summary: Counts “human beings” taken as spoil from Midian, a similar war-spoil tally.

1-chronicles-5:22:0.summary: “With us is the Lord our God… to fight our war” matches “the war was from God.”
1-chronicles-5:22:0.why: Same conviction that God owns the war.

1-chronicles-5:22:1.summary: The Lord fighting for Israel so one pursues a thousand is a general divine-warrior theme.

1-chronicles-5:22:2.summary: “If God is for us, who is against us?” is a general theme of God’s support.

1-chronicles-5:22:3.summary: Thaglathphellasar takes Gilead and deports the people, the “deportation” that ended their settlement.

1-chronicles-5:22:4.summary: The Assyrian deportation of Israel to Abor and Gozan matches the deportation ending their stay.

1-chronicles-5:22:5.summary: A Levitical genealogy line (Elkanah, Souphi, Naath) has no connection to the war or deportation.

1-chronicles-5:22:6.summary: Simeonites strike others and “settled in their place,” the same phrase used of the Transjordan tribes.

1-chronicles-5:23:0.summary: Names Hermon and its other name Senir, matching “Sanir, and Mount Aermon.”

1-chronicles-5:23:1.summary: “Senir and Hermon” with Lebanon match the same northern landmarks of Manasseh’s land.

1-chronicles-5:23:2.summary: “All Mount Hermon, and all Bashan” defines the same region the half-tribe occupied.

1-chronicles-5:23:3.summary: Records the half-tribe of Manasseh’s inheritance in “all the kingdom of Bashan.”

1-chronicles-5:23:4.summary: Shares only the name Hermon in a poetic image of dew; no link to Manasseh’s settlement.

1-chronicles-5:24:0.summary: Similar formula of “rulers” in “ancestral houses” who multiplied, a generic genealogical phrase.

1-chronicles-5:25:0.summary: Israel mixed with the nations, served their images and “prostituted themselves,” the same unfaithfulness.
1-chronicles-5:25:0.why: Fuller picture of the same apostasy.

1-chronicles-5:25:1.summary: The image of a “mother of prostitutes” loosely echoes spiritual prostitution, without specific link.

1-chronicles-5:25:2.summary: The land will “prostitute itself away from following the Lord,” the same metaphor of whoring after other gods.
1-chronicles-5:25:2.why: Prophetic use of the same image.

1-chronicles-5:25:3.summary: Israel “prostituted yourself away from your God,” matching going whoring after the peoples’ gods.

1-chronicles-5:25:4.summary: Warns that inhabitants of the land would “prostitute themselves to their gods,” the snare the tribes fell into.

1-chronicles-5:25:5.summary: Israel followed the nations “whom the Lord removed before” them and feared other gods, explaining the exile.
1-chronicles-5:25:5.why: Same cause for the northern deportation.

1-chronicles-5:25:6.summary: Israel “prostituted themselves after other gods” and abandoned their fathers’ way, the same apostasy.

1-chronicles-5:25:7.summary: Jacob forsook God and turned to foreign gods unknown to their fathers, the same breach of faith.
1-chronicles-5:25:7.why: Song of Moses foresaw this apostasy.

1-chronicles-5:25:8.summary: They forsook “the God of their fathers” and followed “gods of the peoples,” closely matching the source.

1-chronicles-5:25:9.summary: Amaziah worships gods of a conquered people, a general idolatry parallel.

1-chronicles-5:25:10.summary: Israel “prostituted themselves after the Baalim,” the same image of whoring after gods.

1-chronicles-5:26:0.summary: Phul king of the Assyrians is the same as Phaloch king of Assour named in the source.

1-chronicles-5:26:1.summary: Thaglathphellasar takes Gilead and deports the people, the deportation of the Transjordan tribes.
1-chronicles-5:26:1.why: Kings’ account of the same event.

1-chronicles-5:26:2.summary: Deportation to Alae, Abor and “rivers of Gozan” matches Chalach, Chabor and the River Gozan.

1-chronicles-5:26:3.summary: Repeats the exile to Alae, “the Abor, the river of Gozan,” the same destinations as the source.

1-chronicles-5:26:4.summary: The Lord brings Assyrian commanders against King Manasseh, a different event with a similar theme of God using Assyria.

1-chronicles-5:26:6.summary: Gozan is named among nations destroyed by Assyria, sharing only the place.

1-chronicles-5:26:7.summary: God summons armed nations to fulfill His wrath, a general theme of God stirring foreign powers.

1-chronicles-5:26:8.summary: Ahaz appeals to Thaglathphellasar, the same Assyrian king God stirred up.

1-chronicles-5:26:9.summary: Gozan appears among lands destroyed by Assyria, a place-name overlap only.

1-chronicles-5:26:10.summary: The Lord incites David against Israel, a loose parallel of God moving a king’s will.

1-chronicles-5:26:11.summary: Assyria as “the rod of My anger” sent against His people matches God stirring Assyria’s kings to deport Israel.
1-chronicles-5:26:11.why: Theology of Assyria as God’s tool.

1-chronicles-5:26:12.summary: Those “whose spirit God had stirred” echo God stirring “the spirit” of Assyrian kings, here for return rather than exile.
1-chronicles-5:26:12.why: Same idiom of God stirring spirits.

1-chronicles-5:27:1.summary: Same three sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath and Merari (Gedson, Kaath, Merari).

1-chronicles-5:27:3.summary: Identical list “Gedson, Kaath, and Merari” used for David’s service courses.

1-chronicles-5:27:0.summary: Lists Levi’s sons Gershon, Kohath and Merari, the same three names.

1-chronicles-9:22:1.why: Shows David’s ordering of Levite offices.
1-chronicles-9:22:1.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-9:22:2.summary: Service courses for ministry in the Lord’s house relate only generally to the gatekeepers’ appointment.

1-chronicles-9:22:3.summary: Same chapter’s Korite Levite assigned a task; only the context is shared.

1-chronicles-9:22:4.summary: A note on Levite portions in Benjamin shares no element with the gatekeepers’ count.

1-chronicles-9:22:5.summary: David appoints singers rather than gatekeepers; shared only Davidic appointment of Levites.
1-chronicles-9:22:5.why: Parallel Davidic appointment of a Levite guild.

1-chronicles-9:22:6.summary: Singers’ farmsteads rest on the Hebrew “villages”; the Greek-based source says “courts.”
1-chronicles-9:22:6.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.
1-chronicles-9:22:6.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-9:22:7.summary: Netophati villages echo the Hebrew “villages”; the Saints source reads “courts.”
1-chronicles-9:22:7.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording absent here.

1-chronicles-9:22:8.summary: Lists “the divisions of the gates,” the gatekeepers whose number and appointment the source gives.
1-chronicles-9:22:8.why: Roster of the same gatekeeper divisions.

1-chronicles-9:22:9.summary: Continues with “their brethren in their courts” and gatekeepers serving “in faithfulness.”
1-chronicles-9:22:9.why: Immediate continuation of the same description.

1-chronicles-9:22:10.summary: Judahite farmstead towns share no element with the gatekeepers in their courts.

1-chronicles-9:22:11.summary: Shares the word “faithfully” for Levite duties but describes distribution, not gatekeeping.
1-chronicles-9:22:11.why: Similar language of faithful Levite service.

1-chronicles-9:22:12.summary: Appointing men over treasury chambers is a general parallel to appointing gatekeepers.

1-chronicles-9:22:13.summary: Service courses ready for ministry shares only general Levitical organization.

1-chronicles-9:22:14.summary: Shares the distinctive pairing of “enrollment” and “faithfulness” for Levite records.
1-chronicles-9:22:14.why: Chronicler’s idiom for faithful Levite registration.

1-chronicles-9:23:0.summary: Levites assigned to “keep the duties of the house” loosely parallels guard duty at the house’s gates.
1-chronicles-9:23:0.why: Prophetic picture of Levite house duties.

1-chronicles-9:23:1.summary: Levites serving “as gatekeepers at the house’s gates” directly matches the source’s gate duties.
1-chronicles-9:23:1.why: Prophetic restatement of the gatekeeper role.

1-chronicles-9:23:2.summary: “The gatekeepers stood at the gates of the Lord’s house,” matching guard over the gates in the Lord’s house.
1-chronicles-9:23:2.why: Shows gatekeepers at work under Jehoiada.

1-chronicles-9:23:3.summary: Levites “kept the charges” and watched over gatekeepers by David’s commandments.

1-chronicles-9:23:4.summary: Levites “keep the charges of the Tent of Testimony” in the Lord’s house, echoing the tent-house guard.
1-chronicles-9:23:4.why: Links guard duty to the Tent’s charges.

1-chronicles-9:24:0.summary: Gate lots fall east, north, south, and west, matching gates “toward the four winds.”

1-chronicles-9:25:0.summary: A Sabbath-based guard rotation loosely parallels brethren coming in for seven-day turns.
1-chronicles-9:25:0.why: Shows weekly guard shifts in practice.

1-chronicles-9:25:1.summary: Divisions serving Sabbath to Sabbath loosely parallels seven-day rotations.
1-chronicles-9:25:1.why: Shows weekly division shifts in practice.

1-chronicles-9:25:2.summary: Divisions going out on the Sabbath to guard the Lord’s house relates to rotating duty.
1-chronicles-9:25:2.why: Shows weekly guard shifts in practice.

1-chronicles-9:26:0.summary: Levites bring tithes “to the treasuries in God’s house,” with gatekeepers present.
1-chronicles-9:26:0.why: Shows the treasuries the Levites oversaw.

1-chronicles-9:26:1.summary: A large “treasury chamber” stored provisions for Levites and gatekeepers.
1-chronicles-9:26:1.why: Illustrates the temple chambers in Levite care.

1-chronicles-9:26:2.summary: Hezekiah’s tithe collection relates to temple stores; the shown text does not mention chambers or treasuries.
1-chronicles-9:26:2.why: Background on what the treasuries held.

1-chronicles-9:26:3.summary: “The Levites… were over the treasuries of the Lord’s house” matches the source almost verbatim.
1-chronicles-9:26:3.why: Davidic assignment of the same treasury duty.

1-chronicles-9:27:0.summary: Levites stand in the morning and keep the Tent’s charges; daily morning duty is a loose parallel.
1-chronicles-9:27:0.why: Shows the daily rhythm of Levite service.

1-chronicles-9:27:1.summary: A general exhortation to serve shares no specific element with temple gatekeeping.

1-chronicles-9:27:2.summary: Temple doors being shut in rebuke is only incidental to opening doors each morning.

1-chronicles-9:27:3.summary: Samuel “opened the doors of the Lord’s house” in the morning, the same daily task.

1-chronicles-9:28:0.summary: Men appointed over treasury chambers relates loosely to Levites over the ministry vessels.

1-chronicles-9:28:1.summary: Mentions temple “vessels” stored in a treasury chamber; no counting is shown.
1-chronicles-9:28:1.why: Shows where temple vessels were kept.

1-chronicles-9:28:2.summary: Ezra weighs out silver, gold, and holy “vessels” to be guarded and accounted for.
1-chronicles-9:28:2.why: Illustrates careful accounting of temple vessels.

1-chronicles-9:28:3.summary: Balak and Balaam’s dialogue has no link to temple vessels or counting.

1-chronicles-9:28:4.summary: Levites over the treasuries of holy things relate generally to custody of temple goods.
1-chronicles-9:28:4.why: General Levite custody of holy things.

1-chronicles-9:29:0.summary: Levites handle “the fine flour of the sacrifice,” matching the fine flour in their charge.
1-chronicles-9:29:0.why: Davidic assignment of the same supplies.

1-chronicles-9:29:1.summary: Pure olive oil for the lamp relates only to the oil among the supplies.
1-chronicles-9:29:1.why: Origin of the sanctuary oil supply.

1-chronicles-9:29:2.summary: Prescribes the sanctuary “spices” and anointing oil, supplies the Levites were appointed over.
1-chronicles-9:29:2.why: Origin of the spices and oil in Levite care.

1-chronicles-9:30:0.summary: Holy oil from “spices” made by “a perfumer’s skill” matches the priests’ perfumers.
1-chronicles-9:30:0.why: Origin of the priestly perfumers’ task.

1-chronicles-9:30:1.summary: Compounded incense as “the pure work of a perfumer” matches the priests’ perfuming role.
1-chronicles-9:30:1.why: Shows the perfumer’s craft in the sanctuary.

1-chronicles-9:30:3.summary: Forbids copying the holy oil, implying only authorized makers; perfumers are not named.
1-chronicles-9:30:3.why: Explains why priests alone compounded it.

1-chronicles-9:31:0.summary: Introduces “Salom son of Kore… the Korites,” the father of Mattathias.

1-chronicles-9:31:1.summary: Same chapter on Levite appointments, without naming Salom or Mattathias.

1-chronicles-9:31:2.summary: Names “Salom” as ruler of the gatekeepers, Mattathias’ father.

1-chronicles-9:31:3.summary: Levites over chambers and treasuries forms the context of Mattathias’ trust.

1-chronicles-9:31:4.summary: Describes a grain “sacrifice from a griddle,” the pan offering Mattathias prepared.

1-chronicles-9:31:5.summary: A grain offering from a hearth relates only loosely to the pan offering.

1-chronicles-9:32:1.summary: Gives the genealogies of “Kaath’s sons,” the clan of Banaias the Kaathite.

1-chronicles-9:32:2.summary: Commands “the bread of the Presence” on the table continually, the loaves Banaias prepared.

1-chronicles-9:33:0.summary: David appoints “singers” and Heman “the psalm singer” to minister in the Lord’s house.
1-chronicles-9:33:0.why: Origin of the psalm singers’ office.

1-chronicles-9:33:1.summary: Levites appointed to praise and sound trumpets “continually,” paralleling work day and night.

1-chronicles-9:33:2.summary: Servants who stand in the Lord’s house bless the Lord “by night.”

1-chronicles-9:33:3.summary: Lists the divisions of temple singers, the psalm singers the source summarizes.

1-chronicles-9:33:4.summary: Calls those standing in the Lord’s house to praise; only general theme is shared.

1-chronicles-9:33:5.summary: Tax exemption for singers and Levites relates only loosely to their dedicated service.

1-chronicles-9:33:6.summary: The “Levites’ rulers” appoint “the psalm singers” with instruments.
1-chronicles-9:33:6.why: Shows how the singers were appointed.

1-chronicles-9:33:7.summary: Names Mathania son of Micha, an Asaphite singer from the earlier list; the source names no one.
1-chronicles-9:33:7.why: Example of a singer in the roster.

1-chronicles-9:33:8.summary: Asaphite singers over work of the house under “the king’s command”; general overlap.

1-chronicles-9:34:0.summary: Both speak of “rulers of ancestral houses” serving the house of God.
1-chronicles-9:34:0.why: Echoes the summary of the priestly heads.

1-chronicles-9:34:1.summary: “The rulers of the people lived in Jerusalem,” paralleling the Jerusalem settlement roster.
1-chronicles-9:34:1.why: Parallel account of who dwelt in Jerusalem.

1-chronicles-9:35:0.summary: Repeats the Gabaon genealogy: “In Gabaon dwelt the father of Gabaon; his wife’s name was Maacha.”
1-chronicles-9:35:0.why: Parallel version of Saul’s family tree.

1-chronicles-9:35:1.summary: Uses the same “father of” a town formula, but for unrelated Calebite clans.

1-chronicles-9:35:2.summary: Shares only the “father of” a town formula (Galaad’s father, Thekoe’s father).

1-chronicles-9:35:3.summary: “Maon was Baithsour’s father” uses the same town-founder formula only.

1-chronicles-9:36:0.summary: Continues the same list: “Ner begot Kish; Kish begot Saul.”

1-chronicles-9:36:1.summary: The parallel genealogy names Ner, Kish, and Saul from the same family.
1-chronicles-9:36:1.why: Parallel version of the Saulide line.

1-chronicles-9:37:0.summary: “Gedour, his brother, Zachour, and Makaloth” parallels the source list.

1-chronicles-9:38:0.summary: Nearly identical: “Makaloth begot Semaa… dwelt… in Jerusalem, with their brethren.”

1-chronicles-9:39:5.summary: Names Saul’s sons Jonathan and Melchisa and that “Kish was Saul’s father.”

1-chronicles-9:39:0.summary: Mentions Saul and his son Jonathan, but only in passing.
1-chronicles-9:39:0.why: Brief narrative mention of Saul and Jonathan.

1-chronicles-9:39:1.summary: Jonathan, Aminadab, and Melchisa, “Saul’s sons,” die in battle.
1-chronicles-9:39:1.why: Records the fate of the sons listed.

1-chronicles-9:39:3.summary: Introduces “Jonathan son of Saul” in a battle episode; only the person is shared.

1-chronicles-9:39:4.summary: Jonathan, Amminadab, and Melchisoue, “Saul’s sons,” are struck down.
1-chronicles-9:39:4.why: Records the fate of the sons listed.

1-chronicles-9:40:0.summary: “The sons of Jonathan: Meribaal. Meribaal begot Michia” parallels the source.

1-chronicles-9:40:1.summary: Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth is the Maribaal of the genealogy under another name.

1-chronicles-9:41:0.summary: “The sons of Michia: Phithon, Melchel, Theree” parallels Phaithon, Malach, Tharach.

1-chronicles-9:42:0.summary: “Achaz begot Joiada; Joiada begot Galemath, Asmoth, and Zambri” parallels the source.

1-chronicles-9:43:0.summary: “Maisa begot Baana; Raphaia was his son, Elasa… Esel” matches the source.

1-chronicles-9:1:8.summary: Jeremiah 39:9 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
1-chronicles-9:1:8.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
1-chronicles-9:1:8.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

1-chronicles-10:1:1.summary: The later verse finds Saul and his sons “fallen on Mount Gelboue,” the same battle.

1-chronicles-10:1:2.summary: Saul’s army camps at “Gilboa” before the battle against the foreigners.
1-chronicles-10:1:2.why: Shows the setup for the battle.

1-chronicles-10:1:3.summary: The messenger finds Saul on “Mount Gilboa” closed in by enemies, the same defeat.
1-chronicles-10:1:3.why: Gives the report of the same battle.

1-chronicles-10:1:4.summary: David’s lament curses the “Mountains in Gilboa” where Saul fell.
1-chronicles-10:1:4.why: Shows David’s grief over this defeat.

1-chronicles-10:1:5.summary: The foreigners gather at Aphek before the war, but the text shows David, not the battle.
1-chronicles-10:1:5.why: Gives background to the same campaign.

1-chronicles-10:1:6.summary: The foreigners gather “to go out and fight with Israel,” the start of this campaign.
1-chronicles-10:1:6.why: Gives background to the same campaign.

1-chronicles-10:1:7.summary: The text recalls “the day the foreigners struck Saul down at Gilboa,” this same battle.
1-chronicles-10:1:7.why: Shows the later burial of Saul’s bones.

1-chronicles-10:2:0.summary: Isaiah speaks generally of the righteous perishing; nothing ties it to Saul’s sons.

1-chronicles-10:2:1.summary: The genealogy lists Saul’s sons “Jonathan, Melchisoue, Amminadab,” the three killed here.

1-chronicles-10:2:2.summary: Saul swears that Jonathan must die for a broken oath; only the names are shared.

1-chronicles-10:2:3.summary: The list of “Saul’s sons” includes Jonathan and Melchisa, the Melchisoue here.

1-chronicles-10:2:4.summary: The genealogy lists Saul’s sons “Jonathan, Melchisoue, Amminadab,” the three killed here.

1-chronicles-10:2:5.summary: Jonathan’s earlier victory shows the same son, but the event is unrelated.

1-chronicles-10:2:6.summary: King Josiah is killed in battle by a foreign king, a loose parallel.
1-chronicles-10:2:6.why: Shows another king falling in battle.

1-chronicles-10:2:7.summary: The commandment on fathers’ sins is not suggested by the account of Saul’s sons dying.

1-chronicles-10:2:8.summary: Sedekias’s sons are killed by the enemy, a loose parallel to Saul’s sons.
1-chronicles-10:2:8.why: Shows another dynasty ending in defeat.

1-chronicles-10:3:1.summary: The Amalekite reports that “Saul also died, and Jonathan his son” on Gilboa.
1-chronicles-10:3:1.why: Gives a second report of the same battle.

1-chronicles-10:3:2.summary: Amos says “the mighty one will certainly not maintain his strength,” a general image of defeat.
1-chronicles-10:3:2.why: Shows the theme of a warrior’s defeat.

1-chronicles-10:3:3.summary: Joseph is attacked by “masters of arrows,” sharing only the image of archers.

1-chronicles-10:4:9.summary: The next verse tells that the armor-bearer “too fell on his sword and died.”

1-chronicles-10:4:1.summary: Judas falls headlong in a field; there is no sword or similar act.

1-chronicles-10:4:2.summary: Ahithophel takes his own life after defeat, a loose parallel to Saul.

1-chronicles-10:4:3.summary: The jailer “drew his sword” to kill himself, a similar but separate act.

1-chronicles-10:4:4.summary: David fears the “uncircumcised” foreigners will rejoice over Saul, echoing Saul’s fear of their mockery.
1-chronicles-10:4:4.why: Shows that Saul’s fear of shame came true.

1-chronicles-10:4:5.summary: Zimri kills himself when his city is taken, a loose parallel.

1-chronicles-10:4:6.summary: Judas “hanged himself,” another suicide but with no other link.

1-chronicles-10:4:7.summary: David calls Goliath an “uncircumcised” foreigner; only the term is shared.

1-chronicles-10:4:8.summary: Samson fears falling “into the hand of the uncircumcised,” like Saul’s fear.
1-chronicles-10:4:8.why: Shows the same fear of the enemy.

1-chronicles-10:4:10.summary: The foreigners capture and abuse Samson, the kind of humiliation Saul feared.
1-chronicles-10:4:10.why: Shows what capture by the foreigners meant.

1-chronicles-10:4:12.summary: Jonathan speaks to the one “carrying his equipment” about “uncircumcised men,” but in a different event.

1-chronicles-10:4:13.summary: The Amalekite claims Saul asked him to “put me to death,” a different version of this death.
1-chronicles-10:4:13.why: Gives a conflicting account of Saul’s death.

1-chronicles-10:4:14.summary: The foreigners mock Samson before Dagon, the mockery Saul feared.
1-chronicles-10:4:14.why: Shows what capture by the foreigners meant.

1-chronicles-10:4:15.summary: Abimelech also asks his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say…”
1-chronicles-10:4:15.why: Close parallel to a king avoiding disgrace.

1-chronicles-10:4:16.summary: David executes the man who claimed to kill “the Lord’s anointed,” the aftermath of Saul’s death.
1-chronicles-10:4:16.why: Shows David’s response to Saul’s death.

1-chronicles-10:6:0.summary: Ecclesiastes reflects on one fate for all; nothing ties it to Saul’s house.

1-chronicles-10:6:1.summary: Samuel warns that “both you and your king” will be swept away if Israel does evil.
1-chronicles-10:6:1.why: Shows the warning behind Saul’s fall.

1-chronicles-10:6:2.summary: Hosea says God gave a king “in My anger,” a general comment on kingship.
1-chronicles-10:6:2.why: Shows a prophetic view of Saul’s kingship.

1-chronicles-10:6:3.summary: Israel is defeated and Eli’s two sons die on one day, a loose parallel.
1-chronicles-10:6:3.why: Shows another house falling in one day.

1-chronicles-10:6:4.summary: Eli dies on the day of defeat, a loose parallel to a leader’s fall.
1-chronicles-10:6:4.why: Shows another leader dying with his house.

1-chronicles-10:7:1.summary: “The men of Israel saw” their danger and hid, a similar reaction in another war.
1-chronicles-10:7:1.why: Shows a similar reaction to defeat.

1-chronicles-10:7:2.summary: The curse of fleeing from enemies loosely matches Israel’s flight here.
1-chronicles-10:7:2.why: Shows the covenant curse of defeat.

1-chronicles-10:7:3.summary: The sojourner rising above Israel loosely matches foreigners taking the cities.
1-chronicles-10:7:3.why: Shows the covenant curse of defeat.

1-chronicles-10:7:4.summary: Israel flees Midian to caves and strongholds, a similar flight in another war.
1-chronicles-10:7:4.why: Shows a similar reaction to defeat.

1-chronicles-10:7:5.summary: The curse of desolate cities loosely matches Israel abandoning its cities.
1-chronicles-10:7:5.why: Shows the covenant curse of defeat.

1-chronicles-10:7:6.summary: A foreign nation consuming Israel’s land loosely matches the foreigners taking the cities.
1-chronicles-10:7:6.why: Shows the covenant curse of defeat.

1-chronicles-10:8:1.summary: Jehoshaphat’s people “came to plunder,” a similar act in another battle.

1-chronicles-10:8:2.summary: Moab rushes “to the spoils,” a similar act in another battle.

1-chronicles-10:9:0.summary: David says not to “proclaim good news” among the foreigners, the very news sent out here.
1-chronicles-10:9:0.why: Shows David’s lament over this news.

1-chronicles-10:9:2.summary: John the Baptist’s head is carried off, a loose parallel to Saul’s head being taken.

1-chronicles-10:9:3.summary: Belshazzar praises idols with temple vessels; there is no specific link to Saul.

1-chronicles-10:9:4.summary: Captured vessels are used before idols, loosely like spoils announced to idols.

1-chronicles-10:9:5.summary: The foreigners praise their god for giving Samson “into our hand,” as they report Saul’s fall to their idols.
1-chronicles-10:9:5.why: Shows the foreigners crediting their gods for victory.

1-chronicles-10:9:6.summary: The earlier verse shows Saul fearing the “uncircumcised” would mock him; here they take his body.

1-chronicles-10:10:1.summary: The ark is placed in “Dagon’s house,” where Dagon’s own head is severed, the same temple.
1-chronicles-10:10:1.why: Shows the irony of Saul’s head in Dagon’s house.

1-chronicles-10:11:0.summary: “The men of Jabesh in Gilead buried Saul,” the sequel to Galaad hearing of his death.
1-chronicles-10:11:0.why: Shows how the men of Galaad responded.

1-chronicles-10:11:1.summary: Saul rescues Jabesh-gilead from Nahash, which explains why the people of Galaad honored him.
1-chronicles-10:11:1.why: Explains Jabesh’s loyalty to Saul; the range is truncated.

1-chronicles-10:12:0.summary: David fasts in mourning for Abner, a loose parallel to the seven-day fast.
1-chronicles-10:12:0.why: Shows fasting as mourning for a leader.

1-chronicles-10:12:1.summary: David takes Saul’s and Jonathan’s bones from “the men of Jabesh-gilead” and reburies them.
1-chronicles-10:12:1.why: Shows what later became of these bones.

1-chronicles-10:12:2.summary: Joseph mourns his father “seven days,” sharing only the length of mourning.

1-chronicles-10:12:3.summary: Deborah is buried “under the oak,” sharing only the image of burial beneath an oak.

1-chronicles-10:13:0.summary: The law condemns anyone who follows “spirit mediums,” the sin named in Saul’s death.

1-chronicles-10:13:1.summary: The law forbids following “spirit mediums,” the practice Saul turned to.

1-chronicles-10:13:2.summary: Samuel tells Saul that because he “treated the Lord’s word as nothing,” he will not be king.
1-chronicles-10:13:2.why: Gives the earlier verdict on Saul.

1-chronicles-10:13:3.summary: Isaiah rebukes those who consult “belly-speakers” and “seek the dead” instead of God, as Saul did.
1-chronicles-10:13:3.why: Shows the prophetic view of consulting the dead.

1-chronicles-10:13:5.summary: The law forbids anyone who “is a medium” or “inquires of the dead,” as Saul did.

1-chronicles-10:13:6.summary: The law against sorcerers is related to Saul’s sin, but does not mention mediums.

1-chronicles-10:13:7.summary: The command against Amalek was the word Saul later failed to keep, but this text does not say so.

1-chronicles-10:13:8.summary: Manasseh also uses divination and “knowing ones,” a similar sin by a later king.
1-chronicles-10:13:8.why: Shows another king condemned for this sin.

1-chronicles-10:13:9.summary: Samuel tells Saul “you have not kept my commandment,” the failure named here.
1-chronicles-10:13:9.why: Gives the earlier verdict on Saul.

1-chronicles-10:13:10.summary: A girl has “a spirit of divination,” sharing only the general theme of spirits.

1-chronicles-10:13:11.summary: Simon’s magic shares only the general theme of occult practice.

1-chronicles-10:13:12.summary: Sirach recalls that Samuel, after death, “showed the king his end,” the answer Saul received.

1-chronicles-10:14:0.summary: Samuel says the Lord “has torn Israel’s kingdom” from Saul to give it to another.
1-chronicles-10:14:0.why: Gives the earlier word now fulfilled.

1-chronicles-10:14:1.summary: Samuel says Saul’s kingdom “will not stand” and God will appoint another ruler.
1-chronicles-10:14:1.why: Gives the earlier word now fulfilled.

1-chronicles-10:14:2.summary: God sends Samuel to “Jesse” to find a king to replace Saul.
1-chronicles-10:14:2.why: Shows the choice of David son of Jesse.

1-chronicles-10:14:4.summary: The army comes to David “to turn Saul’s kingdom over to him,” using the same expression.
1-chronicles-10:14:4.why: Shows how the transfer took place.

1-chronicles-10:14:5.summary: Abner vows “to remove the kingdom from Saul’s house and raise up David’s throne.”
1-chronicles-10:14:5.why: Shows the transfer of the kingdom.

1-chronicles-10:14:6.summary: Saul “inquired through the Lord” but got no answer, which Chronicles contrasts with not seeking Him.
1-chronicles-10:14:6.why: Adds the other side of the story.

1-chronicles-10:14:7.summary: The proverb about repaying evil has no specific link to Saul or David.

1-chronicles-10:14:8.summary: Israel forsakes the Lord and is told to seek other gods, a loose parallel.
1-chronicles-10:14:8.why: Shared theme only; the range is truncated.

1-chronicles-10:14:9.summary: The image of an ax and saw has no clear link to Saul’s fall.
