1-chronicles-16:16:13.summary: Sirach says God established the covenant with Isaac “because of Abraham his father,” matching the source.
1-chronicles-16:16:13.why: Parallel summary of the patriarchal covenant.

1-chronicles-16:16:0.summary: God says “I will set My covenant” with Abraham, the covenant the source recalls.
1-chronicles-16:16:0.why: Origin of the covenant with Abraham.

1-chronicles-16:16:2.summary: God’s blessing to Jacob is related, but the source verse concerns Abraham and Isaac.

1-chronicles-16:16:3.summary: Paul discusses the covenant and promises spoken “to Abraham,” the same covenant recalled in the source.
1-chronicles-16:16:3.why: New Testament reading of the Abrahamic covenant.

1-chronicles-16:16:4.summary: “The Lord made a covenant with Abram,” the very covenant the source recalls.

1-chronicles-16:16:5.summary: “God of Abraham … Isaac” names the same patriarchs but does not mention covenant or oath.

1-chronicles-16:16:6.summary: Zechariah recalls God remembering “His holy covenant, the oath He swore to Abraham,” echoing the psalm.
1-chronicles-16:16:6.why: New Testament echo of covenant and oath.

1-chronicles-16:16:7.summary: God’s oath “By Myself I have sworn” to Abraham at the binding of Isaac is the oath the source recalls.

1-chronicles-16:16:8.summary: Nehemiah’s prayer recalls God making “a covenant with him” (Abraham) to give the land.
1-chronicles-16:16:8.why: Later retelling of the Abrahamic covenant.

1-chronicles-16:16:9.summary: Peter cites “the covenant God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham.”
1-chronicles-16:16:9.why: Apostolic use of the Abrahamic covenant.

1-chronicles-16:16:10.summary: God’s promise of land to Abram is part of the covenant recalled in the psalm.

1-chronicles-16:16:11.summary: Hebrews explains God’s promise and oath to Abraham, swearing by Himself (shown text only).

1-chronicles-16:16:12.summary: God of Abraham and Isaac renews the promise to Jacob; relevant to the next verse more than this one.

1-chronicles-16:17:6.summary: Shares the phrase “everlasting covenant,” but with David rather than Jacob/Israel.

1-chronicles-16:17:0.summary: God establishes His covenant “as an everlasting covenant” with Abraham’s seed, including the land of Canaan.

1-chronicles-16:17:1.summary: God confirms to Jacob/Israel the land given to Abraham and Isaac, the covenant passed to Jacob.
1-chronicles-16:17:1.why: Narrative of covenant confirmed to Jacob.

1-chronicles-16:17:2.summary: Joshua recounts the fulfilment of the land gift, related but not about establishing the covenant.

1-chronicles-16:17:3.summary: Shares “everlasting covenant,” but it concerns David’s blessings, not Jacob.

1-chronicles-16:17:4.summary: Israel “did not keep God’s covenant,” contrasting with God’s faithfulness; shared word only.

1-chronicles-16:17:5.summary: “Eternal covenant” in Christ’s blood shares the phrase but not the patriarchal context.

1-chronicles-16:17:7.summary: God’s promise to bring Israel into the land of the Canaanites relates loosely to the covenant.
1-chronicles-16:17:7.why: Land promise reaffirmed at the Exodus.

1-chronicles-16:17:8.summary: “The words of this covenant” in Jeremiah refers to the Sinai covenant, not the patriarchal one; only an incidental word.

1-chronicles-16:18:0.summary: God tells Abram “all the land … I will give to you,” the land promise the source quotes.

1-chronicles-16:18:1.summary: God setting bounds of nations loosely relates to the allotted inheritance, without mention of Canaan.

1-chronicles-16:18:2.summary: Dividing the land as “inheritance” by lot relates to the measured allotment, but at a later stage.

1-chronicles-16:18:3.summary: God tells Jacob “I will give this land” to him and his seed, the promise the source quotes.

1-chronicles-16:18:4.summary: “The land on which you sleep I will give to you” is the land promise to Jacob.

1-chronicles-16:18:5.summary: “To your seed I will give this land” matches the promise quoted in the source.

1-chronicles-16:18:6.summary: Both promise to give “the land of Canaan” as a lasting possession.

1-chronicles-16:18:7.summary: Micah’s “measuring cord by lot” echoes the measured allotment, but as a threat of losing it.

1-chronicles-16:19:0.summary: Jacob says “I am few in number” among the Canaanites, matching the patriarchs being few.

1-chronicles-16:19:1.summary: God chose Israel though they were “the fewest of all the nations.”

1-chronicles-16:19:2.summary: The patriarchs confessed they were “strangers and sojourners,” matching dwelling as strangers in the land.
1-chronicles-16:19:2.why: New Testament reflection on patriarchal sojourning.

1-chronicles-16:19:3.summary: Abraham received no inheritance yet was promised it, loosely matching living as strangers in the land.

1-chronicles-16:20:0.summary: God sends Jacob to Egypt; related to wandering among nations but without the travel itself.
1-chronicles-16:20:0.why: Background to the move to Egypt.

1-chronicles-16:20:1.summary: Jacob and his seed entering Egypt is an instance of traveling “from nation to nation.”

1-chronicles-16:20:2.summary: Abram going down into Egypt is an instance of the patriarchs’ wanderings among nations.

1-chronicles-16:20:3.summary: Abraham journeyed and lived as a stranger in Gerar, an example of moving among peoples.

1-chronicles-16:21:1.summary: God afflicted Pharaoh because of Sara, an instance of reproving kings on the patriarchs’ account.

1-chronicles-16:21:2.summary: Laban had power to harm Jacob but God warned him, showing no one allowed to overpower them.

1-chronicles-16:21:3.summary: Moses confronting Pharaoh shows God opposing a king, but it is later than the patriarchal setting (shown text only).
1-chronicles-16:21:3.why: Later example of God opposing a king.

1-chronicles-16:21:4.summary: God warned Laban in a dream, “Take care not to speak evil to Jacob,” protecting Jacob.

1-chronicles-16:21:5.summary: God’s message to Pharaoh shows Him confronting a king, but not in the patriarchal era (shown text only).
1-chronicles-16:21:5.why: Later example of God opposing a king.

1-chronicles-16:21:6.summary: Jacob says God “rebuked you yesterday,” referring to Laban, matching God reproving others for His people.
1-chronicles-16:21:6.why: Narrative of God rebuking Jacob’s oppressor.

1-chronicles-16:22:2.summary: Jacob’s blessing of Judah mentions no anointed ones or prophets and has no real link to the command.

1-chronicles-16:22:3.summary: Shares the ideas of anointing and a “prophet,” but Elijah’s commission is unrelated to protecting the patriarchs.

1-chronicles-16:22:4.summary: The believers’ “anointing” in John is an incidental word match, not a link to God’s protected anointed ones.

1-chronicles-16:22:5.summary: Jacob blessing Ephraim and Manasseh has no anointing, prophets or protection language.

1-chronicles-16:22:6.summary: Isaac’s blessing of Esau has no connection to touching God’s anointed or prophets.

1-chronicles-16:23:1.summary: Both speak of proclaiming God’s salvation continually: “Thy salvation all day.”
1-chronicles-16:23:1.why: Echo of daily proclamation of salvation.

1-chronicles-16:23:2.summary: God’s salvation lasting “through generations of generations” relates loosely to proclaiming it day to day.

1-chronicles-16:23:3.summary: “Sing the Lord’s name … announce these throughout the earth” parallels singing and proclaiming in all the earth.

1-chronicles-16:23:4.summary: The psalmist “spoke of … Thy salvation” before the congregation, like proclaiming His salvation.

1-chronicles-16:23:5.summary: “Sing praise to the Lord” is a common call to praise without the universal or salvation elements.

1-chronicles-16:23:6.summary: Earlier in the same hymn: “Sing unto Him and hymn Him,” recounting His wonders to everyone.

1-chronicles-16:23:7.summary: Miriam’s “Let us sing to the Lord” is a general song of praise, not the universal call.
1-chronicles-16:23:7.why: Early example of singing to the Lord.

1-chronicles-16:25:3.summary: Both call God “great and fearsome above all,” a close verbal echo.

1-chronicles-16:25:0.summary: The song of Moses and the Lamb praises God as “Great” and asks “Who shall not fear,” echoing great and fearsome.
1-chronicles-16:25:0.why: Heavenly echo of praise of God’s greatness.

1-chronicles-16:25:1.summary: “How fearsome are Thy works” shares the fearsome theme but not the comparison with gods.

1-chronicles-16:25:2.summary: The shown verse describes silver-and-gold idols, only loosely relating to God above all gods (truncated range).
1-chronicles-16:25:2.why: Contrasts idols with the true God.

1-chronicles-16:25:4.summary: The psalm on man’s frailty and God’s descent shares no specific element with God’s greatness over gods.

1-chronicles-16:25:5.summary: “Who is like Thee among the gods, O Lord?” matches God being fearsome above all gods.

1-chronicles-16:25:6.summary: “Thou art fearsome” shares one attribute but lacks the comparison with gods.

1-chronicles-16:25:7.summary: Isaiah’s questions about God’s greatness over creation and nations parallel only the general theme (truncated range).

1-chronicles-16:25:8.summary: “Will you not fear Me?” relates to God being fearsome, but in a rebuke over creation’s order.

1-chronicles-16:26:0.summary: “The heavens are works of Thy hands” parallels “our God made heaven.”

1-chronicles-16:26:1.summary: The Lord “who made heaven” matches the same confession of God as Creator.

1-chronicles-16:26:2.summary: “I stretched heaven alone” affirms the Lord alone made heaven, as against idols.

1-chronicles-16:26:3.summary: The command not to follow “idols” shares the idol theme but not the creation contrast.

1-chronicles-16:26:4.summary: God displaying the heavenly host relates loosely to God making heaven.

1-chronicles-16:26:5.summary: Paul teaches that “things made by hands are not gods,” matching that the nations’ gods are idols.

1-chronicles-16:26:6.summary: Isaiah’s satire on those who “fashion a god” shows the nations’ gods are mere made things (shown text).

1-chronicles-16:26:7.summary: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold” directly matches “all the nations’ gods are idols.”
1-chronicles-16:26:7.why: Close parallel on the nations’ idols.

1-chronicles-16:26:8.summary: Worship “the One who made heaven” echoes God as maker of heaven.
1-chronicles-16:26:8.why: Creator as the true object of worship.

1-chronicles-16:26:9.summary: “An idol is nothing … there is no God except one” restates the contrast between idols and God.

1-chronicles-16:26:10.summary: “Gods who did not make heaven and earth” perish, while the Lord stretched out heaven—same contrast.

1-chronicles-16:27:1.summary: Gladness “in Thy presence” relates loosely to glory and praise before Him.

1-chronicles-16:27:2.summary: God as “my strength” and His holy dwellings loosely echo strength in His place.

1-chronicles-16:27:3.summary: The Lord as “stronghold” of His people shares only a general strength theme.

1-chronicles-16:27:4.summary: Seeing God’s “power and Thy glory” in the holy place parallels glory and strength in His place.
1-chronicles-16:27:4.why: God’s glory and power in the sanctuary.

1-chronicles-16:27:5.summary: Praise of God’s wondrous name and magnificence shares only the theme of glory.

1-chronicles-16:27:6.summary: Desire to dwell in the Lord’s house and sing relates loosely to praise in His place.

1-chronicles-16:27:7.summary: Beholding Christ’s “glory” shares only the word glory.

1-chronicles-16:28:0.summary: Paul’s testimony of grace has nothing to do with giving glory and strength to the Lord.

1-chronicles-16:28:1.summary: Paul’s strength through Christ is unrelated to the nations ascribing strength to God.

1-chronicles-16:28:2.summary: “Shout to the Lord, all the earth” is a general universal call to worship.

1-chronicles-16:28:3.summary: Power made complete in weakness shares only the word “power,” not the liturgical call.

1-chronicles-16:28:4.summary: Incidental words “glory” and “strength” in Paul’s prayer do not echo the call to give God glory.

1-chronicles-16:28:5.summary: “Bring to the Lord … bring to the Lord glory and honor” is the same liturgical formula.

1-chronicles-16:28:6.summary: “Give glory to His praise” and “all the earth” share general praise language.

1-chronicles-16:28:7.summary: Giving glory to God’s name, not to ourselves, shares the glory theme loosely.

1-chronicles-16:28:8.summary: “Give glory to God … His power” closely parallels giving the Lord glory and strength.
1-chronicles-16:28:8.why: Parallel ascription of glory and power.

1-chronicles-16:28:9.summary: David ascribes to God “greatness, power, glory … and strength,” as the hymn calls the nations to do (shown text).
1-chronicles-16:28:9.why: David’s own ascription of glory and strength.

1-chronicles-16:28:10.summary: “All the nations … will come and bow down … and glorify Thy name” matches the nations giving God glory.

1-chronicles-16:28:11.summary: “The praise of the glory of His grace” is only incidental wording, unrelated to the nations’ worship.

1-chronicles-16:28:12.summary: Nations hoping in Jesse’s root relates loosely to nations turning to God.

1-chronicles-16:28:13.summary: “Shout to God, all the earth” is a general universal call to praise.

1-chronicles-16:28:14.summary: “Let all earth’s ends fear Him” relates generally to the nations honoring God.

1-chronicles-16:28:15.summary: “Let nations rejoice” shares the theme of nations worshiping God.

1-chronicles-16:29:0.summary: Entering “His courts” with hymns and praising “His name” parallels worship in His holy courts.

1-chronicles-16:29:2.summary: The seraphim’s praise of God’s holiness and glory shares only general worship themes.
1-chronicles-16:29:2.why: Heavenly worship of the Holy One.

1-chronicles-16:29:3.summary: “Holiness and magnificence are in His sanctuary” relates to worship in His holy place, though it parallels the hymn’s earlier verse.

1-chronicles-16:29:4.summary: Praising God among nations and exalting His glory is a general parallel.

1-chronicles-16:29:5.summary: “Let us come before His face with thanksgiving” loosely parallels bringing gifts before Him.

1-chronicles-16:29:6.summary: “Bring to the Lord glory for His name; bow down to the Lord in His holy courtyard” is nearly identical.

1-chronicles-16:29:7.summary: Gold given to the king loosely parallels bringing gifts, but the recipient is the king.

1-chronicles-16:29:8.summary: Heavenly beings give glory and the elders fall and worship, loosely matching glory and bowing before the Lord.

1-chronicles-16:29:9.summary: God “glorified in the council of holy ones” shares only the general theme of glory.
1-chronicles-16:29:9.why: God’s glory among the holy ones.

1-chronicles-16:29:10.summary: Singers praise “the holy things” and give thanks to the Lord, a loose worship parallel.

1-chronicles-16:29:11.summary: “Splendors of the holy ones” assumes a shared phrase (beauty of holiness) that the source’s “holy courts” does not carry.

1-chronicles-16:29:12.summary: “Let them praise the Lord’s name” shares the theme of glorifying His name.

1-chronicles-16:29:13.summary: Ascribing “glory … power and strength” to God is a general heavenly doxology.
1-chronicles-16:29:13.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-16:29:14.summary: God taking away Israel’s strength and boasting has no link to bringing gifts and worshiping.

1-chronicles-16:29:15.summary: The “splendor of His beauty” from Zion depends on a Hebrew phrase not present in the source’s wording.
1-chronicles-16:29:15.why: No real connection in this wording.

1-chronicles-16:29:16.summary: Worthy to receive “glory” and the elders’ worship form a general heavenly doxology.

1-chronicles-16:29:17.summary: Kings “will bring gifts,” matching “take gifts and bring them before Him.”

1-chronicles-16:29:18.summary: Ornaments turned into abominable images have no real link to bringing gifts to the Lord.

1-chronicles-16:29:19.summary: Nations bringing gold and offerings to God’s altar and house parallel bringing gifts before Him.

1-chronicles-16:29:20.summary: Foreigners praying toward the temple relates loosely to nations worshiping in God’s courts.

1-chronicles-16:29:21.summary: Envoys from Egypt and Ethiopia coming to God loosely parallels nations bringing gifts.

1-chronicles-16:30:0.summary: Creation by God’s command relates only generally to the earth being set right.

1-chronicles-16:30:1.summary: Christ “upholding all things” loosely parallels the earth being set right and not shaken.

1-chronicles-16:30:2.summary: God “established them for the age,” loosely matching a stable, set-right earth.

1-chronicles-16:30:3.summary: The Lord’s reign over the world relates to the hymn’s kingship theme but not this verse’s wording.

1-chronicles-16:30:4.summary: “He established the inhabited world, which will not be shaken” closely matches the verse.
1-chronicles-16:30:4.why: Close parallel on a stable world.

1-chronicles-16:30:5.summary: The Servant given “to establish the earth” shares a word but in a different sense.
1-chronicles-16:30:5.why: Related idea of establishing the earth.

1-chronicles-16:30:6.summary: Same hymn calls God “fearsome above all the gods,” the basis for the earth’s fear.

1-chronicles-16:30:7.summary: Same hymn addresses “all the earth,” a contextual link only.
1-chronicles-16:30:7.why: Same hymn’s address to the earth.

1-chronicles-16:30:9.summary: The Lord “set the inhabited world upright,” matching the earth being “set right and not be shaken.”

1-chronicles-16:30:10.summary: “In Him all things hold together” loosely parallels a stable, unshaken earth.

1-chronicles-16:31:1.summary: “The Lord has become King!” with the earth addressed echoes the proclamation “The Lord reigns!”

1-chronicles-16:31:2.summary: The heavenly multitude cries that “the Lord God Almighty hath reigned,” echoing “The Lord reigns!”

1-chronicles-16:31:3.summary: “The Lord has become King! Let the earth exult” closely matches the verse.

1-chronicles-16:31:4.summary: “The Lord reigned” and the unshaken world echo this and the preceding verse.

1-chronicles-16:31:5.summary: “All the earth … exult” is a general call to joyful praise.

1-chronicles-16:31:6.summary: “Rejoice, heavens, and let earth exult!” closely parallels “Let heaven be glad and the earth exult.”

1-chronicles-16:31:7.summary: Praising God as “my King” shares only the kingship theme.

1-chronicles-16:31:8.summary: Good news of joy “for all the people” loosely parallels rejoicing among nations.

1-chronicles-16:31:9.summary: The heavens declaring God’s glory share only the theme of heaven praising God.

1-chronicles-16:31:10.summary: Joy in heaven over a repentant sinner has no real link to the proclamation of God’s reign.

1-chronicles-16:31:11.summary: The heavens acknowledging God’s wonders is a general heavenly-praise parallel.

1-chronicles-16:31:12.summary: “The Lord our king” shares the kingship theme only.

1-chronicles-16:31:13.summary: The heavens are called to praise the Lord, a general cosmic-praise theme.

1-chronicles-16:31:14.summary: “Rejoice, heavens … earth’s foundations” calls heaven and earth to joy, as the verse does.

1-chronicles-16:31:15.summary: The shown Lord’s Prayer petition about temptation has no link to God’s reign or cosmic joy.

1-chronicles-16:31:16.summary: Heaven’s praise and “on earth peace” loosely pair heaven and earth in praise.
1-chronicles-16:31:16.why: Heaven and earth joined in praise.

1-chronicles-16:32:0.summary: “Let the sea be shaken, and all that fills it” matches the sea resounding with its fullness.

1-chronicles-16:32:1.summary: Mountains, hills “and all their trees” cry out joy, like the trees of the field rejoicing.

1-chronicles-16:32:2.summary: The roaring sea’s surges relate loosely to the sea resounding.
1-chronicles-16:32:2.why: Sea as witness to God’s majesty.

1-chronicles-16:32:3.summary: Trees and creatures listed among those praising God share a general creation-praise theme.

1-chronicles-16:33:1.summary: “For He has come to judge the earth” is identical wording in the parallel psalm.

1-chronicles-16:33:2.summary: Awaiting the Lord’s coming relates only generally to His coming to judge.

1-chronicles-16:33:3.summary: God reigning and the time for judgment loosely parallel His coming to judge the earth.

1-chronicles-16:33:4.summary: “All the plain’s trees will know” the Lord shares the image of trees responding to God.

1-chronicles-16:33:5.summary: Christ’s coming with vengeance relates to coming judgment, but with no joy or creation imagery.

1-chronicles-16:33:6.summary: “When He comes” to be glorified shares only the idea of the Lord’s coming.

1-chronicles-16:34:5.summary: The temple singers say “Give thanks to the Lord, for it is good, for His mercy endures for ever.”
1-chronicles-16:34:5.why: Same refrain at the temple dedication.

1-chronicles-16:34:1.summary: Israel praises: “For it is good, for His mercy endures for ever.”

1-chronicles-16:34:2.summary: At the temple’s founding they sing “For it is good, for His mercy … endures for ever.”

1-chronicles-16:34:3.summary: “Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good; His mercy is for ever” is the same refrain.

1-chronicles-16:34:4.summary: The psalm repeats “Give thanks to the Lord … for His mercy is for ever” throughout (shown text).

1-chronicles-16:34:6.summary: Jeremiah foresees voices saying “Give thanks to the Lord Almighty, for the Lord is good; His mercy is for ever.”

1-chronicles-16:34:7.summary: “Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy is for ever” is the same refrain.

1-chronicles-16:35:1.summary: God’s people proclaiming His excellences loosely parallels praising His holy name after rescue.

1-chronicles-16:35:2.summary: “Help us, God our Savior … rescue us” for His name’s sake, with the nations, closely parallels the plea.

1-chronicles-16:35:3.summary: God’s people acquired to recount His praiseworthy deeds loosely matches the purpose of praise.

1-chronicles-16:35:4.summary: Believers as a spiritual house offering sacrifices has no specific link to the plea for rescue.

1-chronicles-16:35:5.summary: Longing for “Israel’s salvation” and return from captivity loosely parallels rescue from the nations.

1-chronicles-16:35:6.summary: Being “to the praise of His glory” shares only the general goal of praising God.

1-chronicles-16:35:7.summary: Israel “will be glorified” in God loosely echoes glorying in His praises.

1-chronicles-16:35:8.summary: A purpose clause about keeping God’s law at the end of the parallel psalm shares no specific wording.

1-chronicles-16:35:9.summary: “Boast in the Lord” loosely echoes glorying in God’s praises.

1-chronicles-16:35:10.summary: The hymn opened with “Praise in His holy name,” which this closing plea echoes.
1-chronicles-16:35:10.why: Frames the hymn’s beginning and end.

1-chronicles-16:35:11.summary: Hope for “Israel’s salvation” and return from captivity loosely parallels rescue from the nations.

1-chronicles-16:35:12.summary: “In Thy name we will give thanks for ever” matches praising His holy name and glorying in Him.

1-chronicles-16:36:0.summary: “Blessed be the Lord God, the God of Israel … for the age … May it be!” matches the doxology.

1-chronicles-16:36:1.summary: Solomon says “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,” the same doxology formula.

1-chronicles-16:36:2.summary: “Blessed be the Lord” is a common formula; the context of rest is different.

1-chronicles-16:36:3.summary: Esdras blessed the Lord and “All the people answered and said, ‘Amen,’” as in the source.
1-chronicles-16:36:3.why: Same people’s Amen after a blessing.
1-chronicles-16:36:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-16:36:4.summary: “Blessed be the God” shares the blessing formula in a Christian setting.

1-chronicles-16:36:5.summary: The link assumes Jeremiah’s “Amen,” but the Saints text reads “Truly!,” so no shared Amen is present.

1-chronicles-16:36:6.summary: “Blessed be the God and Father” shares the blessing formula only.

1-chronicles-16:36:7.summary: Paul refers to saying “the Amen” to a blessing, the same congregational practice.

1-chronicles-16:36:9.summary: “All the people shall … say: So be it” mirrors “All the people shall say, ‘Amen’” (shown text).
1-chronicles-16:36:9.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-16:37:0.summary: Levites minister “according to each day’s requirement” following David’s ordinance, continuing this arrangement.

1-chronicles-16:37:1.summary: “Each day’s due on its own day” matches “each day’s duty on its day.”

1-chronicles-16:37:2.summary: David appoints “the sons of Asaph” for musical service, the same Asaph and brethren (shown text).

1-chronicles-16:37:4.summary: Asaph son of Barachia and his brethren are appointed as singers before the ark (shown text).

1-chronicles-16:38:0.summary: Osa of Merari’s sons is the gatekeeper Ossa named in the source.

1-chronicles-16:38:1.summary: God’s ark stayed in Abeddara’s house, the same Abdedom later serving as gatekeeper.
1-chronicles-16:38:1.why: Background on Abdedom and the ark.

1-chronicles-16:38:2.summary: Abdedom’s sons and brethren, “sixty-two in all,” parallel “Abdedom and his brethren, sixty-eight.”

1-chronicles-16:38:3.summary: Idithon and his sons are named, the same Idithon whose son Abdedom is mentioned.

1-chronicles-16:39:5.summary: “The bama in Gabaon … the Tent of Testimony” is the same tent-shrine where Sadok served.

1-chronicles-16:39:0.summary: Solomon sacrifices at Gibeon’s great high place, the same shrine at Bama in Gabaon.

1-chronicles-16:39:1.summary: David summons “Sadok … the priests,” the same Sadok left at Gabaon.

1-chronicles-16:39:2.summary: A “Sadok, a young man mighty in strength” may be the same Sadok, but the text does not say he is a priest.

1-chronicles-16:39:4.summary: “The Lord’s tent … in Bama at Gabaon” names the very same tent and location.
1-chronicles-16:39:4.why: Explains why the tent was at Gabaon.

1-chronicles-16:40:2.summary: “Continual offering of whole burnt offerings morning and evening” matches the source’s daily offerings.

1-chronicles-16:40:4.summary: Hezekiah funds “the morning and evening burnt offerings … written in the Lord’s law,” the same ordinance.
1-chronicles-16:40:4.why: Later observance of the daily offerings.

1-chronicles-16:40:1.summary: The law prescribes lambs “in the morning and … in the evening” as “a continual offering,” the law the source cites.
1-chronicles-16:40:1.why: The written law behind the practice.

1-chronicles-16:40:3.summary: The returned exiles offer a whole burnt offering “in the morning and toward evening.”

1-chronicles-16:40:5.summary: Mentions the time “for the sacrifice to go up,” only a passing allusion to the daily offering.
1-chronicles-16:40:5.why: Daily sacrifice as a time marker.

1-chronicles-16:40:6.summary: “Sacrifices for the morning” at Bethel are condemned as lawless, contrasting with lawful offerings.

1-chronicles-16:40:7.summary: “The hour of the evening sacrifice” refers to the daily offering only as a time marker.

1-chronicles-16:40:8.summary: Ezekiel prescribes a “daily burnt offering” and “continual burnt offering” each morning.
1-chronicles-16:40:8.why: Daily offering in Ezekiel’s temple vision.

1-chronicles-16:41:0.summary: Singers praise the Lord, saying “for His mercy endures for ever,” the same refrain and role.
1-chronicles-16:41:0.why: Same singers’ refrain in the temple.

1-chronicles-16:41:1.summary: David appoints the sons of “Aiman, and Idithon” to praise the Lord, the same musicians (shown text).

1-chronicles-16:41:2.summary: Appointed singers praise, saying “Give thanks to the Lord, for His mercy is for ever.”

1-chronicles-16:41:3.summary: “Heman the psalm singer” is the same singer called Aiman in the source.

1-chronicles-16:41:4.summary: Israel praises the Lord “for His mercy endures for ever,” the same refrain.

1-chronicles-16:41:5.summary: Men “called by name” shares a phrase but concerns the census leaders.

1-chronicles-16:41:7.summary: The Lord’s mercy “from eternity to eternity” echoes the refrain’s theme loosely.

1-chronicles-16:41:8.summary: Praise “for His mercy toward Israel endures for ever” repeats the refrain.

1-chronicles-16:41:9.summary: Jeremiah foresees voices saying “His mercy is for ever” in praise.

1-chronicles-16:41:10.summary: The preceding verse sets Asaph and his brethren before the ark; the same musicians’ arrangement continues.

1-chronicles-16:41:11.summary: Asaph’s and Ethan’s genealogies concern the singers’ families, but Aiman and Idithon are not named in the shown text.

1-chronicles-16:41:12.summary: “His mercy is for generations” loosely echoes the everlasting-mercy refrain.

1-chronicles-16:41:13.summary: Nathinim “gathered by name” shares a phrase but concerns temple servants.

1-chronicles-16:41:14.summary: Men “designated by name” shares a phrase but concerns soldiers.

1-chronicles-16:42:1.summary: Praise with “trumpet” and “cymbals” mirrors the instruments used for God’s songs.

1-chronicles-16:42:3.summary: Levites with cymbals and “David’s instruments” and priests with trumpets continue this arrangement (shown text).

1-chronicles-16:42:0.summary: The link assumes a “doorkeeper,” but the Saints text reads “cast aside in the house of God,” with no gate.
1-chronicles-16:42:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-16:42:2.summary: Singers with cymbals under “Asaph, Idithon, and Aiman” describe the same musical service.

1-chronicles-16:42:4.summary: Levites had “instruments for the Lord’s songs” and priests sounded trumpets, matching the verse.

1-chronicles-16:43:1.summary: After the festival the people “went, each to his tent” and were blessed, a parallel conclusion.
1-chronicles-16:43:1.why: Parallel close of a great celebration.

1-chronicles-16:43:2.summary: Abraham directing his household shares only the theme of a leader’s household.

1-chronicles-16:43:3.summary: Walking in innocence “within my house” loosely relates to David returning to his household.

1-chronicles-16:43:4.summary: “I and my house will serve the Lord” shares only a household-faith theme.

1-chronicles-17:1:0.summary: David made houses for himself and a tent for God’s ark, the contrast he now voices.
1-chronicles-17:1:0.why: Background of David’s house and the ark’s tent.

1-chronicles-17:1:1.summary: Solomon recalls it came upon David’s heart “to build a house for the name of the Lord.”

1-chronicles-17:1:2.summary: God replies that He has dwelt “in a tent,” answering David’s concern about the ark’s covering.
1-chronicles-17:1:2.why: God’s answer in the same oracle.

1-chronicles-17:1:3.summary: The link assumes cedar palaces, but the Saints text of Jeremiah has no cedar or house wording.

1-chronicles-17:1:4.summary: The ark was set “inside the tent David had pitched for it,” the tent David now contrasts with his house.

1-chronicles-17:1:5.summary: David vows to find “a dwelling for the God of Jacob,” the same concern for the ark.

1-chronicles-17:1:6.summary: The ark placed under the tent covering explains its curtained setting, a loose background link.
1-chronicles-17:1:6.why: Origin of the ark’s tent covering.

1-chronicles-17:1:7.summary: Haggai contrasts living in fine houses while God’s house is waste, the same contrast David feels.

1-chronicles-17:1:8.summary: Nebuchadnezzar at peace in his house shares only an incidental setting.

1-chronicles-17:1:9.summary: Nebuchadnezzar’s boast about Babylon has no real link to David’s concern for the ark.

1-chronicles-17:1:10.summary: “My house is desolate, while each of you hurries to his own house” parallels David’s contrast.

1-chronicles-17:1:11.summary: Names “Nathan the prophet,” the same person, but in an unrelated episode.

1-chronicles-17:1:12.summary: Chiram sent “cedar wood” to build David a house, the cedar house David mentions.

1-chronicles-17:1:14.summary: Names “Nathan the prophet” in an unrelated episode.

1-chronicles-17:1:15.summary: Mentions “the records of Nathan the prophet,” a source for David’s reign.

1-chronicles-17:1:16.summary: Names “Nathan the prophet” in Solomon’s succession story only.

1-chronicles-17:1:17.summary: David brought God’s ark up and “prepared a tent for it in Jerusalem,” the ark under skins.

1-chronicles-17:1:19.summary: Nathan the prophet comes to David, the same pair, but in the rebuke over Bathsheba.

1-chronicles-17:1:20.summary: God’s ark was set “in the middle of the tent David had pitched for it,” the tent now contrasted.

1-chronicles-17:1:21.summary: Names “Nathan the prophet” before King David in a later episode.

1-chronicles-17:2:0.summary: David recalls “It came upon my heart to build a house of rest for the ark,” the plan Nathan endorses.
1-chronicles-17:2:0.why: David’s own account of his intent.

1-chronicles-17:2:1.summary: “We … prophesy in part” could illustrate Nathan’s initial answer, but the link is interpretive.

1-chronicles-17:2:2.summary: “Do everything your hand finds, for God is with you” closely matches Nathan’s words.

1-chronicles-17:2:3.summary: “God is with you” is shared, but the context is the nations seeking Israel.

1-chronicles-17:2:4.summary: Leaders acting without inquiring of the Lord may illustrate Nathan’s hasty answer; interpretive link.

1-chronicles-17:2:5.summary: “May He give you according to your heart” loosely echoes “Do everything in your soul.”

1-chronicles-17:2:6.summary: God seeing differently from humans could illustrate Nathan’s human judgment; only a loose link.

1-chronicles-17:2:7.summary: David tells Solomon “it came upon my soul to build a house,” the desire Nathan endorses.
1-chronicles-17:2:7.why: David’s own account of his intent.

1-chronicles-17:2:9.summary: “The Lord is with you” is a shared phrase in a different setting.

1-chronicles-17:3:0.summary: God revealing His purposes to “His servants the prophets” relates generally to the word coming to Nathan.

1-chronicles-17:3:1.summary: In the Saints text the words heard are from those who led astray, unrelated to the Lord’s word to Nathan.

1-chronicles-17:3:2.summary: “The Lord’s word came” to Isaiah after his first message, a similar pattern of revised prophecy (shown text).
1-chronicles-17:3:2.why: Prophet sent back with a new word.

1-chronicles-17:3:3.summary: God speaking to a prophet “in sleep” loosely relates to the word coming at night.

1-chronicles-17:4:0.summary: David recalls God saying “You shall not build Me a house,” the same divine word.

1-chronicles-17:4:2.summary: God’s ways being higher than human plans loosely fits God overruling David’s plan.

1-chronicles-17:4:3.summary: “You shall not build the house; your son … shall build” restates this decree.

1-chronicles-17:4:4.summary: God’s unsearchable ways and counsel loosely relate to His refusal of David’s plan.

1-chronicles-17:4:6.summary: “You will not build the house. Your son … will build” restates the same decree.

1-chronicles-17:5:1.summary: “What sort of house will you build for Me?” shares the house-for-God theme with a different emphasis.
1-chronicles-17:5:1.why: God not confined to a house.

1-chronicles-17:5:2.summary: “Since the day I brought My people Israel out … I chose no city … to build a house” parallels the verse.

1-chronicles-17:5:3.summary: Solomon asks who can build God a house, a related but different point about God’s greatness.

1-chronicles-17:5:4.summary: Erecting “the Tent of Testimony” for the ark is the tent in which God says He dwelt.

1-chronicles-17:5:5.summary: The ark set “inside the tent David had pitched” shows God still dwelling in a tent.

1-chronicles-17:5:6.summary: The “tent of testimony” brought into the temple relates loosely to God’s tent dwelling.

1-chronicles-17:5:7.summary: “Will God truly dwell with people on earth?” relates to God’s dwelling but makes a different point.

1-chronicles-17:5:8.summary: “Will God indeed dwell with men upon earth?” shares the dwelling theme with a different emphasis.

1-chronicles-17:6:1.summary: The ark went ahead of Israel on its journeys, illustrating God passing through all the places.

1-chronicles-17:6:2.summary: “You shall shepherd My people Israel” uses the same shepherding-leader language.

1-chronicles-17:6:3.summary: God raising “shepherds” for His people shares the shepherd-leader image generally.

1-chronicles-17:6:4.summary: Christ walking among the lampstands has no real link to God not demanding a cedar house.

1-chronicles-17:6:5.summary: The judges God raised are a likely referent, but the Saints text speaks of a “tribe” appointed to shepherd.

1-chronicles-17:6:6.summary: “I will walk among you” relates to God moving among Israel, without the house theme.

1-chronicles-17:6:7.summary: God walking “in the midst of your camp” loosely parallels God passing through Israel.

1-chronicles-17:6:8.summary: God’s cloud over the tent “throughout all their journeys” illustrates His moving dwelling.

1-chronicles-17:6:9.summary: A ruler who will “shepherd his flock” shares the shepherd image only.

1-chronicles-17:6:10.summary: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” relates loosely to God’s presence rather than a house.

1-chronicles-17:6:11.summary: Mentions the era of “judges until Samuel,” only background to the leaders referred to.

1-chronicles-17:6:12.summary: God promising to go before Israel relates loosely to His passing through Israel.

1-chronicles-17:6:13.summary: God took David “to shepherd Jacob His people,” the same shepherd-ruler language.

1-chronicles-17:6:14.summary: “Shepherd My people Israel” is shared, but applied to the Messiah from Bethlehem.
1-chronicles-17:6:14.why: Messianic use of the shepherd phrase.

1-chronicles-17:6:15.summary: “Shepherds of Israel” are rebuked, sharing only the shepherd-leader image.

1-chronicles-17:6:16.summary: Lists leaders God sent before the monarchy, loosely relating to those appointed to shepherd.

1-chronicles-17:7:0.summary: David says God chose him “to appoint me ruler over His people, over Israel.”
1-chronicles-17:7:0.why: David’s own testimony of his calling.

1-chronicles-17:7:1.summary: Moses called while tending sheep is a similar pattern, but a different person (shown text).

1-chronicles-17:7:3.summary: David “is tending the flock” when called and anointed, the event God recalls.
1-chronicles-17:7:3.why: Narrative of David taken from the flock.

1-chronicles-17:7:4.summary: Simon’s call from fishing to catching people is only a loose analogy of vocation.

1-chronicles-17:7:6.summary: “The Lord took me from the sheep” and sent Amos to “My people Israel” echo the wording.
1-chronicles-17:7:6.why: Same pattern of calling from the flock.

1-chronicles-17:7:8.summary: Fishermen called from their nets is only a loose analogy of calling from ordinary work.

1-chronicles-17:7:9.summary: A ruler to “shepherd My people Israel” shares the leader-over-Israel theme in a messianic text.

1-chronicles-17:8:0.summary: “The Lord was with him” describes David, as God says “I was with you.”

1-chronicles-17:8:1.summary: Nathan’s “God is with you” anticipates God’s own “I was with you.”

1-chronicles-17:8:2.summary: God raising the poor to sit with rulers loosely parallels David’s rise to greatness.

1-chronicles-17:8:3.summary: “Saul saw that the Lord was with David,” confirming God’s presence with him.

1-chronicles-17:8:4.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us” shares only the general presence theme.

1-chronicles-17:8:5.summary: God increasing greatness and restoring the psalmist is only a loose parallel to David’s name.

1-chronicles-17:8:6.summary: God “raises that one” loosely relates to David’s exaltation.

1-chronicles-17:8:7.summary: “I am with you … wherever you go” closely matches “I was with you wherever you went.”

1-chronicles-17:8:9.summary: David’s song of God subduing his enemies matches “destroyed all your enemies before you.”

1-chronicles-17:8:10.summary: Saul’s death removed David’s rival, but the passage does not speak of God acting for David (shown text).

1-chronicles-17:8:11.summary: David’s spoil from Hadadezer’s cities reflects his victories only indirectly.

1-chronicles-17:8:12.summary: God bringing down rulers and raising the lowly loosely parallels David’s rise.

1-chronicles-17:8:13.summary: David trusting the Lord to deal with Saul relates loosely to God removing his enemies.

1-chronicles-17:8:14.summary: Mighty kings once ruling from Jerusalem loosely reflects the great name given to David.

1-chronicles-17:8:15.summary: The Lord “rescued him from the hand of all his enemies,” matching God destroying David’s enemies.

1-chronicles-17:8:16.summary: David’s response “Thou didst exalt me” relates to God making his name great.
1-chronicles-17:8:16.why: David’s answer in the same chapter.

1-chronicles-17:8:17.summary: “I will love Thee, Lord, my strength” is a general response of trust.

1-chronicles-17:8:18.summary: “The Lord gave David victory wherever he went” matches “I was with you wherever you went.”
1-chronicles-17:8:18.why: Narrative of God’s help in battle.

1-chronicles-17:8:19.summary: “The Lord of powers is with us” shares only the general presence theme.

1-chronicles-17:8:20.summary: “David made a name for himself” and “The Lord gave David victory wherever he went” match both halves.

1-chronicles-17:9:0.summary: Both promise that former distress will be no more, but Revelation speaks of the end of death and tears, not Israel's settled place.
1-chronicles-17:9:0.why: Loose eschatological echo of “no longer” promises.

1-chronicles-17:9:1.summary: Ezekiel promises Israel “will no longer” bear reproach, a general restoration theme close to Israel no longer being humbled.
1-chronicles-17:9:1.why: Shows the same 'no longer oppressed' restoration hope.

1-chronicles-17:9:2.summary: The link relies on “sons of disobedience”, which the Saints source does not contain; it speaks of “Injustice” humbling Israel.
1-chronicles-17:9:2.why: No real connection in the Greek-based wording.

1-chronicles-17:9:3.summary: Israel's groaning under Egyptian labour illustrates the oppression “at the beginning” that God promises will not recur.

1-chronicles-17:9:4.summary: Tyre's self-made wealth has no evident link to God giving Israel a place and planting them.

1-chronicles-17:9:5.summary: God “didst plant our fathers” after casting out nations, the same image of God planting His people in the land.
1-chronicles-17:9:5.why: Recalls the first planting that the promise renews.

1-chronicles-17:9:6.summary: “I will plant them upon their land” and never uproot them closely echoes the promise to plant Israel securely.

1-chronicles-17:9:7.summary: Egyptian forced labour exemplifies the humbling “as at the beginning,” but shares no wording beyond oppression.
1-chronicles-17:9:7.why: Illustrates the past oppression in view.

1-chronicles-17:9:8.summary: Shares the planting image, but the righteous are planted in the Lord's house, not Israel in its land.

1-chronicles-17:9:9.summary: God will “plant them in this land in faithfulness,” a close verbal and thematic echo of planting Israel in its place.
1-chronicles-17:9:9.why: Shows the promise renewed after exile.

1-chronicles-17:9:10.summary: Zion's restored people are “the Lord's planting,” a related image but without the secure-place promise.
1-chronicles-17:9:10.why: General planting metaphor for God's people.

1-chronicles-17:9:11.summary: Depends on “sons of disobedience,” absent from the Saints source, which mentions “Injustice” humbling Israel.
1-chronicles-17:9:11.why: No real link in this wording.

1-chronicles-17:9:12.summary: “Injustice will no longer be heard in your land” closely matches “Injustice shall no longer humble them.”
1-chronicles-17:9:12.why: Strong verbal echo of the peace promise.

1-chronicles-17:9:13.summary: Shown verses promise to rebuild Israel and plant vineyards again, a general restoration echo; the truncated range may hold more.

1-chronicles-17:9:14.summary: God gathers Israel into their own land and feeds them there, akin to appointing them a place but without planting language.

1-chronicles-17:9:15.summary: Those who laid Zion waste depart, loosely matching Israel no longer being humbled by oppressors.

1-chronicles-17:9:16.summary: Israel dwells on its land for ever with “David My servant” ruling, joining the settled-land and Davidic promises of this oracle.
1-chronicles-17:9:16.why: Links the land promise to David's line.

1-chronicles-17:9:17.summary: God will “plant them and certainly not pluck them out,” a clear echo of planting Israel securely.

1-chronicles-17:9:18.summary: In the Davidic covenant psalm, “a son of lawlessness will not go on to harm him” parallels injustice no longer humbling Israel.

1-chronicles-17:10:1.summary: Psalm 89's covenant oracle says “I will cut down his enemies before him,” matching “I humbled all your enemies.”
1-chronicles-17:10:1.why: Psalm's poetic retelling of the promise.

1-chronicles-17:10:2.summary: David praises God for making his enemies turn back and making him “head of nations,” fulfilling the humbling of his enemies.
1-chronicles-17:10:2.why: David's own testimony to the promise.

1-chronicles-17:10:3.summary: Here the midwives “made houses for themselves”; the Greek wording lacks God building a house.
1-chronicles-17:10:3.why: House link does not hold in this text.

1-chronicles-17:10:4.summary: A royal psalm wishing the king's hand to find all his enemies, a general parallel to God humbling David's enemies.

1-chronicles-17:10:5.summary: Describes the period when “the Lord raised up judges” amid enemy oppression, the era the source recalls.

1-chronicles-17:10:6.summary: Christ reigns until all enemies are under His feet, a messianic extension of subduing the king's enemies.

1-chronicles-17:10:7.summary: An example of oppression in the judges period, without shared wording beyond enemies oppressing Israel.

1-chronicles-17:10:8.summary: Philistine domination before David illustrates the enemies later humbled, but no direct link.

1-chronicles-17:10:9.summary: “Unless the Lord builds a house” shares wording, but the psalm speaks generally, not of David's dynasty.
1-chronicles-17:10:9.why: Verbal echo of the Lord building a house.

1-chronicles-17:10:10.summary: God making the Davidic lord's enemies a footstool loosely parallels humbling all David's enemies.

1-chronicles-17:10:11.summary: Israel sold to Chousarsathom in the judges era illustrates oppression, without specific link.

1-chronicles-17:10:12.summary: Philistine invasion in Saul's day shows enemy pressure before David, a loose background link.

1-chronicles-17:10:13.summary: Midianite raids in the judges era illustrate oppression, only generally related.

1-chronicles-17:11:0.summary: The Lord swore to set “from the fruit of your belly” one on David's throne, matching offspring “from your body.”

1-chronicles-17:11:2.summary: “I will raise up a righteous rising for David” echoes “I will raise up your offspring after you.”
1-chronicles-17:11:2.why: Prophetic development of the Davidic heir.

1-chronicles-17:11:3.summary: Jesus “came from David's seed according to the flesh,” the offspring from David's body.
1-chronicles-17:11:3.why: Shows the promise fulfilled in Christ.

1-chronicles-17:11:4.summary: Abraham departs “to your fathers,” the same death idiom but a different person and promise.

1-chronicles-17:11:5.summary: “David lay down with his fathers,” the fulfilment of “you sleep with your fathers.”
1-chronicles-17:11:5.why: Records the predicted death of David.

1-chronicles-17:11:7.summary: David dies and “Solomon his son reigned in his place,” the offspring raised after him.

1-chronicles-17:11:8.summary: Solomon says he has “risen in place of my father David” as the Lord promised.

1-chronicles-17:11:9.summary: Bathsheba speaks of when the king “lies down with his fathers” and Solomon's succession.
1-chronicles-17:11:9.why: Succession crisis tied to the promise.

1-chronicles-17:11:10.summary: Birth of Solomon, the son from David's body whom the Lord loved.

1-chronicles-17:11:11.summary: David reflects that “our days upon earth are as a shadow,” loosely related to his days being fulfilled.

1-chronicles-17:11:12.summary: “You shall sleep with your fathers” is the same death idiom said to Moses, not about David's heir.

1-chronicles-17:11:13.summary: David “fell asleep, was gathered to his fathers,” echoing the promise and contrasting him with the risen heir.

1-chronicles-17:11:14.summary: Peter notes David died and was buried, setting up the promise of a descendant on his throne.
1-chronicles-17:11:14.why: Apostolic reading of the Davidic promise.

1-chronicles-17:12:2.summary: Solomon quotes God's word to David: “Your son... shall build the house for My name.”

1-chronicles-17:12:10.summary: “Build your throne from generation to generation” restates establishing David's heir's throne for ever.

1-chronicles-17:12:0.summary: God sets up a kingdom that stands “for ever,” a general eternal-kingdom theme.

1-chronicles-17:12:1.summary: The child rules “upon the throne of David and his kingdom... for ever,” developing the eternal throne promise.
1-chronicles-17:12:1.why: Messianic extension of the throne promise.

1-chronicles-17:12:3.summary: “Solomon built Him a house,” the fulfilment of “He shall build Me a house.”

1-chronicles-17:12:4.summary: Christ will reign for ages of ages, a general eternal-reign echo.

1-chronicles-17:12:5.summary: David recounts God's word: “Solomon your son will build My house” and “I will set his kingdom upright for ever.”
1-chronicles-17:12:5.why: David's own retelling of the promise.

1-chronicles-17:12:7.summary: David's seed remains for ever and his throne is “established for ever,” matching the throne promise.

1-chronicles-17:12:8.summary: The returned exiles refer to the house “a great king of Israel built,” Solomon's temple.
1-chronicles-17:12:8.why: Later memory of the promised temple.

1-chronicles-17:12:9.summary: The man “Rising” will “build the Lord's house” and “rule on his throne,” echoing the builder-king promise.
1-chronicles-17:12:9.why: Messianic reuse of house and throne.

1-chronicles-17:12:11.summary: “I will establish his seed... and his throne like the days of heaven” parallels the everlasting throne.

1-chronicles-17:12:12.summary: Solomon begins building the Lord's house in Jerusalem, fulfilling “He shall build Me a house.”

1-chronicles-17:12:13.summary: Christ must reign until enemies are subdued, only loosely tied to an eternal throne.

1-chronicles-17:12:14.summary: Jesus speaks of raising the sanctuary of His body, a typological link to the son building God's house.

1-chronicles-17:12:15.summary: Deity dwelling bodily in Christ has no specific link to building a house or establishing a throne.

1-chronicles-17:13:1.summary: “You are My son” echoes “he shall be a son unto Me” for the Davidic king.

1-chronicles-17:13:2.summary: The kingdom torn from Saul is the mercy withdrawn from “those before you.”

1-chronicles-17:13:3.summary: God killed Saul and turned the kingdom to David, the withdrawal contrasted in this verse.

1-chronicles-17:13:4.summary: “I will be a Father to you, and you will be sons” adapts this Father-son promise to believers.
1-chronicles-17:13:4.why: Paul applies the promise to the Church.

1-chronicles-17:13:5.summary: The Greek-based “Take hold of instruction” lacks any “son” wording, so the assumed sonship link is absent.
1-chronicles-17:13:5.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-17:13:6.summary: An everlasting covenant of “the holy and sure blessings of David” echoes God's unwithdrawn mercy to David's heir.
1-chronicles-17:13:6.why: Prophetic recall of the Davidic covenant.

1-chronicles-17:13:7.summary: The preceding verse of the same oracle about the son who builds the house and has an everlasting throne.

1-chronicles-17:13:9.summary: God keeps a scepter for Solomon's son so David has a place always, His mercy not fully withdrawn.
1-chronicles-17:13:9.why: Shows mercy kept despite Solomon's sin.

1-chronicles-17:13:10.summary: The Father loves the Son, a general Father-Son echo without the Davidic setting.

1-chronicles-17:13:11.summary: “Thou art my Father” and “I shall certainly not scatter My mercy away from him” closely retell this verse.
1-chronicles-17:13:11.why: Psalm 89's poetic version of the promise.

1-chronicles-17:13:12.summary: God will not take the whole kingdom from Solomon's son “because of David,” His mercy not withdrawn.

1-chronicles-17:13:13.summary: The voice calls Jesus “My Son,” a general sonship echo.

1-chronicles-17:13:14.summary: Jesus “will be called Son of the Most High” and given “the throne of His father David.”
1-chronicles-17:13:14.why: Annunciation applies the promise to Jesus.

1-chronicles-17:14:0.summary: David's seed remains for ever and “his throne will be like the sun,” matching the everlasting throne.

1-chronicles-17:14:2.summary: The king's name endures “through the ages,” a general royal permanence theme.

1-chronicles-17:14:3.summary: “Christ as a Son over His house” echoes the son made secure “in My house.”
1-chronicles-17:14:3.why: Hebrews applies the house to Christ.

1-chronicles-17:14:4.summary: The king appointed on Zion is a royal theme without the everlasting-throne wording.

1-chronicles-17:15:1.summary: Paul declared the whole purpose of God, loosely like Nathan speaking “all these words.”

1-chronicles-17:15:2.summary: The prophet should tell God's word in truth, generally reflecting Nathan relaying the vision faithfully.

1-chronicles-17:16:1.summary: Paul's “very least of all saints” shares the humble wonder of “Who am I.”

1-chronicles-17:16:2.summary: Jacob's grateful acknowledgment of God's kindness parallels David's humility, without shared wording.

1-chronicles-17:16:3.summary: “What is man, that Thou... takest account of him?” resembles “Who am I... that Thou hast loved me.”

1-chronicles-17:16:4.summary: Saul's protest about his small clan resembles David's “what is my house,” a humility formula.

1-chronicles-17:16:5.summary: “Thus far the Lord has helped us” relies on Hebrew “brought me thus far,” absent from the Saints source.
1-chronicles-17:16:5.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-17:16:6.summary: Jacob praises the God who nourished him all his life, loosely like David's thanks for lasting love.

1-chronicles-17:16:7.summary: Gideon is “small in my father's house,” resembling David's question “what is my house.”
1-chronicles-17:16:7.why: Humility of the one God chooses.

1-chronicles-17:16:8.summary: Hezekiah goes into the Lord's house and lays matters before the Lord, like David sitting before the Lord.

1-chronicles-17:16:9.summary: Deliverance from death has no specific link to David's humble question.

1-chronicles-17:16:10.summary: Paul's testimony “to this day” relies on Hebrew “thus far,” absent from the Saints source.
1-chronicles-17:16:10.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-17:17:0.summary: Comparing small and great things in God's purpose for His servant loosely parallels “These things became small.”
1-chronicles-17:17:0.why: Similar enlargement of a servant's role.

1-chronicles-17:17:1.summary: God “highly exalted” Christ after humility, loosely matching “Thou didst exalt me.”

1-chronicles-17:17:2.summary: These are the promises about David's house “far ahead” to which David responds.

1-chronicles-17:17:3.summary: God chose David from the flocks to shepherd Israel, the exaltation David marvels at.

1-chronicles-17:17:4.summary: God does “far more abundantly than all we ask,” a general echo of God exceeding David's expectations.

1-chronicles-17:17:5.summary: “Thou spakest in a vision” of David, raising “a chosen one,” retells the oracle David praises.

1-chronicles-17:17:6.summary: God took David from the sheepfold and made him a great name, the exaltation David acknowledges.
1-chronicles-17:17:6.why: Earlier part of the same oracle.

1-chronicles-17:17:8.summary: God gives Solomon more than he asked, akin to unexpected favour, but to a different person.

1-chronicles-17:17:9.summary: Nathan reminds David of God's gifts: “If this is little, I will add more,” echoing gifts made “small” before God.
1-chronicles-17:17:9.why: Same prophet, same favour to David.

1-chronicles-17:17:10.summary: “This is a light thing in the eyes of the Lord” resembles “These things became small before Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:18:0.summary: A psalm of David: “Thou didst test me and know me,” echoing “Thou knowest Thy servant.”

1-chronicles-17:18:1.summary: God looks at David's heart at his anointing, loosely tied to God knowing His servant.

1-chronicles-17:18:2.summary: Christ searches hearts, a general divine-knowledge theme.

1-chronicles-17:18:3.summary: “I will honour those who honour Me” relates loosely to David's words on giving glory.
1-chronicles-17:18:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-17:18:4.summary: Peter's “Thou knowest” echoes David's “Thou knowest Thy servant,” in a different setting.

1-chronicles-17:19:0.summary: God acts “because of David My servant”; the Saints source lacks the servant's-sake phrase, leaving a general link.

1-chronicles-17:19:1.summary: The Servant passage shares no specific element with God doing greatness “according to Thy heart.”

1-chronicles-17:19:2.summary: God acting “according to His good pleasure” and “counsel of His will” parallels acting “according to Thy heart.”
1-chronicles-17:19:2.why: God acting from His own will.

1-chronicles-17:19:3.summary: David's later prayer “Thine, O Lord, are greatness” and making things great echoes “all this greatness.”
1-chronicles-17:19:3.why: David's similar praise of God's greatness.

1-chronicles-17:19:4.summary: God's work is “magnificence,” a general praise of His great deeds.

1-chronicles-17:19:5.summary: God's eternal purpose accomplished in Christ loosely parallels God acting by His heart.

1-chronicles-17:19:6.summary: Jacob as God's chosen servant has no specific link to this verse's wording.

1-chronicles-17:19:8.summary: God announced the strength of His works, a general praise of His mighty deeds.

1-chronicles-17:19:9.summary: “For Thy servants' sake” relies on wording absent from the Saints source.

1-chronicles-17:19:10.summary: “This was pleasing before Thee” resembles God acting “according to Thy heart.”

1-chronicles-17:19:11.summary: Israel as the servant in whom God is glorified has no specific link to this verse.

1-chronicles-17:20:8.summary: “There is none holy like the Lord... none holy besides Thee” closely echoes “none like Thee... none besides Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:0.summary: “Apart from Me there is no God” matches “there is none besides Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:1.summary: “Who is like Thee... O Lord?” echoes “there is none like Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:2.summary: God's surpassing power to do more than we ask has no specific link to God's uniqueness here.

1-chronicles-17:20:4.summary: “Lord, God of powers, who is like Thee?” echoes “there is none like Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:5.summary: “There is no god besides Me” matches “none besides Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:6.summary: “There is none like Thee among gods, Lord” echoes “Lord, there is none like Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:9.summary: God leads Moses to make an everlasting name, closer to the next verse than to God's uniqueness here.

1-chronicles-17:20:10.summary: “What god is there... who shall do as Thou hast done” matches God's unrivalled uniqueness.

1-chronicles-17:20:11.summary: “I am God, and there is no other” matches “none besides Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:12.summary: “Before Me no other god came to be” echoes “there is none besides Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:13.summary: “Whatever we heard and knew” from the fathers parallels “according to all we have heard with our ears.”

1-chronicles-17:20:14.summary: “There is none like the God of the beloved” echoes “there is none like Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:20:15.summary: “Who... will be equaled to the Lord?” parallels the confession that none is like Him.

1-chronicles-17:20:16.summary: “To whom did you liken Me?” expresses God's incomparability.

1-chronicles-17:20:17.summary: “God, with our ears we heard” matches “all we have heard with our ears.”

1-chronicles-17:20:18.summary: “To whom did you liken the Lord?” expresses the same incomparability.

1-chronicles-17:20:20.summary: Jethro confesses the Lord is “greater than all gods,” related to but not matching “none besides Thee.”

1-chronicles-17:21:0.summary: God acted for His name among the nations “by bringing them out of Egypt's land,” as in the source.

1-chronicles-17:21:1.summary: God acts “for My name's sake,” but without the exodus or redemption setting.

1-chronicles-17:21:2.summary: “Thou didst redeem Thy people” matches “whom Thou didst redeem.”

1-chronicles-17:21:3.summary: After Egypt, Israel is “a treasured people from among all the nations,” like no nation on earth.

1-chronicles-17:21:4.summary: “Thy hand destroyed nations” and cast them out before Israel parallels “driving nations out.”

1-chronicles-17:21:5.summary: The Lord fought for Israel in conquest, loosely related to driving out nations.

1-chronicles-17:21:6.summary: God “removes great nations from before you,” the driving out of nations the source recalls.

1-chronicles-17:21:7.summary: God's “glorious things” cause trembling, a general echo of His great and manifest deeds.

1-chronicles-17:21:8.summary: God gave Israel the land and rest from enemies, a general fulfilment theme.

1-chronicles-17:21:9.summary: “The Lord your God redeemed you” from Egypt matches “whom Thou didst redeem from Egypt.”

1-chronicles-17:21:10.summary: Those “redeemed by the Lord” praise Him, a general redemption theme.

1-chronicles-17:21:11.summary: “He did not do so for any nation” expresses Israel's unique standing, like “no nation... like Thy people.”

1-chronicles-17:21:12.summary: “He sent redemption to His people” with His fearsome name, a general redemption echo.

1-chronicles-17:21:13.summary: God comes down to rescue Israel from Egypt into the land of the listed nations, the redemption recalled.

1-chronicles-17:21:15.summary: Poetic recall of the sea and Jordan fleeing, a general exodus wonder.

1-chronicles-17:21:16.summary: God's fearsome works, turning sea to dry land, loosely recall the exodus.

1-chronicles-17:21:17.summary: In Egypt “Thou madest a name for Thyself,” matching “to make Himself a great and manifest name.”

1-chronicles-17:21:18.summary: “Who is like unto you, a people saved by the Lord?” and driving out the enemy parallel Israel's uniqueness.

1-chronicles-17:21:19.summary: The Lord “Himself redeemed them,” a general redemption echo.

1-chronicles-17:21:20.summary: God as hope of all earth's ends has no specific link to Israel's redemption from Egypt.

1-chronicles-17:21:21.summary: “What great nation is there whose god draws near” parallels “no nation on the earth like Thy people.”

1-chronicles-17:21:22.summary: God drove out the nations “from before you, not by your sword,” matching driving nations out.
1-chronicles-17:21:22.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

1-chronicles-17:21:23.summary: God led Moses through water “to make Himself an everlasting name,” echoing making Himself a name.

1-chronicles-17:21:24.summary: Christ ransoms “a people for His own possession,” a New Testament echo of redeeming a people.
1-chronicles-17:21:24.why: Redemption theme applied to the Church.

1-chronicles-17:22:0.summary: Israel is made “a treasured people” to God, the basis of being His people.

1-chronicles-17:22:1.summary: The Church is “a people for God's possession,” an extension of Israel's status.

1-chronicles-17:22:2.summary: An “everlasting covenant, to be your God” matches a people “for ever” with the Lord as “their God.”

1-chronicles-17:22:3.summary: Paul affirms God has not rejected His people, loosely tied to Israel being His people for ever.

1-chronicles-17:22:4.summary: “I will be their God, and they will be My people” repeats the covenant formula.

1-chronicles-17:22:5.summary: “This is My people” and “The Lord is my God” echo the covenant formula.

1-chronicles-17:22:6.summary: God chose Israel as “a people for His own possession” and redeemed them, the relation in view.

1-chronicles-17:22:7.summary: God calls “not My people” “My people,” an extension of the people-of-God theme.

1-chronicles-17:22:8.summary: The Lord chose Israel “to be unto Him a people for His own possession.”

1-chronicles-17:22:9.summary: Israel's privileges and covenants are listed, loosely tied to Israel as God's people.

1-chronicles-17:22:10.summary: “The Lord graciously took you to Himself as a people” closely matches “give Thy people... to Thyself.”

1-chronicles-17:23:0.summary: God establishes His oath and Jeremiah answers “May it be, Lord,” loosely like asking God's word be made secure.

1-chronicles-17:23:1.summary: “Remember Thy word to Thy servant” closely echoes “Thy word which Thou didst speak to Thy servant.”

1-chronicles-17:23:2.summary: Jacob reminds God of His promise, a similar prayer pattern without shared wording.

1-chronicles-17:23:3.summary: “May it happen to me according to your word” resembles asking that God's word be fulfilled.

1-chronicles-17:24:0.summary: Jesus prays for the Father's glory, a general theme of God's name glorified.

1-chronicles-17:24:1.summary: God is “called their God,” loosely like people naming the God of Israel.
1-chronicles-17:24:1.why: God named as His people's God.

1-chronicles-17:24:2.summary: “Glorify Thy name” relates loosely; the Saints source has people proclaiming God's title, not magnifying His name.

1-chronicles-17:24:3.summary: “Blessed be His glorious name for the age,” a general praise of God's name.

1-chronicles-17:24:4.summary: “Be exalted, Lord,” a general praise without specific link.

1-chronicles-17:24:5.summary: A prayer for God's splendour on our works has no specific link to David's house being set upright.

1-chronicles-17:24:6.summary: The petition for deliverance from evil has no specific link to this verse.

1-chronicles-17:24:7.summary: Serving so God is glorified through Christ shares nothing specific with this verse.

1-chronicles-17:24:8.summary: Solomon prays that all peoples know God's name as Israel does, loosely like proclaiming the God of Israel.

1-chronicles-17:24:9.summary: Every tongue confesses Christ as Lord, loosely like people declaring “Lord.”

1-chronicles-17:24:10.summary: “Hallowed be Thy name” is a general hope that God's name be honoured.

1-chronicles-17:24:11.summary: God will be “God to Israel's family,” loosely echoing “God of Israel.”

1-chronicles-17:24:12.summary: God dwelling with His peoples as their God loosely echoes the God of Israel theme.

1-chronicles-17:24:13.summary: “I will be their God” is a covenant formula only loosely related to this verse.

1-chronicles-17:25:0.summary: God will “be sought” by Israel to do what He promised, loosely like David praying for the promised house.

1-chronicles-17:25:1.summary: Confidence that God hears requests made according to His will resembles David's courage to pray.

1-chronicles-17:25:2.summary: “The Lord had uncovered Samuel's ear” uses the same idiom as God opening His servant's ear.

1-chronicles-17:25:3.summary: “Thine ear attended” concerns God hearing prayer, not opening the servant's ear.

1-chronicles-17:26:0.summary: God “who does not lie, promised,” a general reliability-of-promise theme.

1-chronicles-17:26:1.summary: It is impossible for God to lie, loosely backing confidence in His good word.

1-chronicles-17:26:2.summary: God's self-revelation as merciful and true loosely grounds trust in His good words.

1-chronicles-17:27:0.summary: God “blessed us with every spiritual blessing,” a general blessing theme.

1-chronicles-17:27:1.summary: God's gifts are irrevocable, loosely like blessing that remains for ever.

1-chronicles-17:27:2.summary: The king's name blessed through the ages loosely echoes David's house blessed for ever.

1-chronicles-17:27:3.summary: Isaac's “blessed him; and let him be blessed” resembles “hast blessed it; bless it for ever,” in another setting.

1-chronicles-17:7:5.summary: 1 Samuel 17:15 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
1-chronicles-17:7:5.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
1-chronicles-17:7:5.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

1-chronicles-17:20:3.summary: Jeremiah 10:6–7 has no corresponding passage in this edition, which follows the Greek text; there is no Saints reading to compare.
1-chronicles-17:20:3.why: Compare a Hebrew-based translation if this passage matters for study.
1-chronicles-17:20:3.note: Passage unavailable in this edition; the review records the absence rather than an interpretation.

1-chronicles-18:1:1.summary: Mentions Gath (the source's Geth) in the ark narrative, sharing only the place.

1-chronicles-18:1:2.summary: David once fled to Gath, the city he now takes, a place link with implicit contrast.

1-chronicles-18:1:3.summary: Gath is named in David's lament, sharing only the Philistine city.

1-chronicles-18:2:0.summary: Kings bring gifts to the ideal king, loosely like Moab bringing gifts to David.

1-chronicles-18:2:1.summary: Kings bring gifts to God at Jerusalem, a general tribute image.

1-chronicles-18:2:2.summary: The queen brings gold and spices to Solomon, a general gift-bearing parallel.

1-chronicles-18:2:3.summary: Balaam's oracle that a man from Israel “shall crush Moab's leaders” finds fulfilment when David strikes Moab.

1-chronicles-18:2:4.summary: “Each brought his gifts” to Solomon, a general tribute parallel.

1-chronicles-18:2:5.summary: Moab is subdued under Israel's hand in Ehud's day, an earlier similar defeat.

1-chronicles-18:2:6.summary: Men refusing gifts to Saul has no specific link to Moab's tribute to David.

1-chronicles-18:2:7.summary: Moab later renders tribute to Israel's king, then rebels, a related but later situation.

1-chronicles-18:2:8.summary: The Greek-based wording (“creeping creatures,” Mount Zion) lacks any Moabite tribute to David.
1-chronicles-18:2:8.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

1-chronicles-18:2:10.summary: God claims Moab and Idumea and subjects the foreigners, the same peoples David subdues here.

1-chronicles-18:2:11.summary: Israel will lay hands on Moab and Idumea, a prophetic echo of subduing Moab.

1-chronicles-18:3:0.summary: The shown text (“Thou didst reject us”) has no link to David's war with Adraazar; any superscription link is not shown.
1-chronicles-18:3:0.why: No link in the shown text.

1-chronicles-18:3:2.summary: God promised borders “to the great river Euphrates,” which David reaches toward here.

1-chronicles-18:3:3.summary: Ammon hires Syrian forces against David; Souba/Zobah is not named in the shown text.

1-chronicles-18:3:4.summary: The land promised “to the great river, the river Euphrates” frames David's push to the Euphrates.

1-chronicles-18:3:5.summary: Saul fought “Zobah's king,” the same kingdom as Souba that David defeats.
1-chronicles-18:3:5.why: Earlier conflict with the same kingdom.

1-chronicles-18:4:1.summary: Trust in God rather than chariots and horses loosely relates to David's captured chariots.

1-chronicles-18:4:2.summary: “A horse is false for salvation” relates loosely to David disabling the chariots.

1-chronicles-18:4:4.summary: Solomon's large chariot force contrasts loosely with David disabling chariots.

1-chronicles-18:4:5.summary: The king must not multiply horses, a possible rationale for David disabling chariots, though not explicit.

1-chronicles-18:4:7.summary: A list of Solomon's officials has nothing to do with David's captured chariots.

1-chronicles-18:5:5.summary: The previous verse introduces David's defeat of Adraazar king of Souba, continued here.

1-chronicles-18:5:0.summary: Ammon hires Syrian forces including Soba, the same Syrian-Souba alliance David fights.
1-chronicles-18:5:0.why: Later phase of the Syrian wars.

1-chronicles-18:5:2.summary: Nations being defeated in general has no specific link to Syria aiding Adraazar.

1-chronicles-18:5:3.summary: Saul fought “Zobah's king,” the kingdom of Adraazar named here.

1-chronicles-18:5:4.summary: Names Hadadezer king of Zobah and Damascus, linking to Adraazar and the Syrians of Damascus here.

1-chronicles-18:6:4.summary: Moab likewise “became servants to David, bringing gifts,” the same formula.

1-chronicles-18:6:0.summary: “I was with you wherever you went” is fulfilled in “The Lord kept saving David in all his journeys.”

1-chronicles-18:6:1.summary: “Help is from the Lord” in war is a general parallel to the Lord saving David.

1-chronicles-18:6:2.summary: David's psalm: God made him “head of nations; a people I did not know served me,” as Syria serves David.

1-chronicles-18:6:3.summary: The Lord guards one's going out, loosely like saving David in all his journeys.

1-chronicles-18:7:0.summary: Mentions the gold items “David had taken from the hands of the servants of Hadadezer” and brought to Jerusalem.

1-chronicles-18:7:1.summary: Sousakim takes gold shields Solomon made, related temple-treasury loss but not David's plunder in this text.

1-chronicles-18:7:2.summary: Solomon makes gold spears and shields, a loose gold-armour parallel.

1-chronicles-18:7:3.summary: Solomon's gold shields form a loose parallel to David's captured gold.

1-chronicles-18:8:1.summary: Describes the pillars, the “one sea,” and the vessels made for Solomon, the very bronze items named.

1-chronicles-18:8:2.summary: David prepared bronze “beyond weighing” for the Lord's house, matching the bronze taken here.

1-chronicles-18:8:4.summary: The Chaldeans carry off the bronze pillars and Sea “which King Solomon made,” the same objects.

1-chronicles-18:8:5.summary: The casting of the bronze pillars for the house's porch, the pillars made from this bronze; range truncated.

1-chronicles-18:10:1.summary: A foreign king sends envoys and gifts to Hezekiah, a general diplomatic parallel.

1-chronicles-18:10:2.summary: Kings bring “silver vessels, gold vessels” to Solomon, a general tribute parallel.

1-chronicles-18:10:3.summary: The queen of Saba visits Solomon with gold, a general foreign-visit parallel.

1-chronicles-18:11:1.summary: Lists Idumeans, Moab, Ammon, Amalek, and foreigners, the same nations named here.

1-chronicles-18:11:0.summary: David earlier raided the Amalekites and took plunder, sharing only Amalek and spoil.

1-chronicles-18:11:4.summary: “These are David's spoils” concerns Amalekite plunder, loosely related.

1-chronicles-18:11:5.summary: Solomon brings in “the holy things of David his father—the silver, the gold,” the consecrated spoil.

1-chronicles-18:11:6.summary: David's huge stores of gold and silver for the Lord's house relate to the spoil he consecrated.

1-chronicles-18:11:7.summary: Israel offers gold and silver for the Tent, a general dedication theme.

1-chronicles-18:11:8.summary: David takes much spoil from the sons of Ammon, one of the nations named here.

1-chronicles-18:11:9.summary: Offering gold, silver, and bronze to the Lord is a general dedication parallel.

1-chronicles-18:11:10.summary: Levites oversee “the treasuries of the consecrated things,” where such dedicated spoil was kept.

1-chronicles-18:11:11.summary: An Amalekite's Egyptian slave has no specific link to consecrating spoil.

1-chronicles-18:11:12.summary: Solomon brings in “the things his father David had consecrated,” the silver and gold dedicated here.

1-chronicles-18:11:13.summary: Later kings' consecrated treasures are given away, a loose consecrated-treasure parallel.

1-chronicles-18:11:14.summary: David acknowledges “of Thine own have we given,” loosely related to dedicating spoil.

1-chronicles-18:11:15.summary: Captured silver and gold “shall be holy to the Lord” in His treasury, a precedent for consecrating spoil.

1-chronicles-18:11:16.summary: Zion will “dedicate their multitude to the Lord,” a prophetic echo of consecrating nations' wealth.

1-chronicles-18:12:3.summary: Amaziah strikes Seir's sons in the “Valley of Salts,” the same place and enemy.
1-chronicles-18:12:3.why: Later battle at the same site.

1-chronicles-18:12:0.summary: The shown text (“Thou didst reject us”) has no link; any Valley of Salt superscription is not shown.
1-chronicles-18:12:0.why: No link in the shown text.

1-chronicles-18:12:1.summary: Abishai, the source's Abessa, leads troops against Ammon.

1-chronicles-18:12:2.summary: Abessa, Joab's brother, commands against Ammon, the same person.

1-chronicles-18:12:5.summary: Identifies Abessa as Zeruiah's son, giving his genealogy.

1-chronicles-18:12:6.summary: Abishai son of Zeruiah volunteers to go with David to Saul's camp.
1-chronicles-18:12:6.why: Earlier exploit of the same man.

1-chronicles-18:12:7.summary: Abessa, Joab's brother, renowned among the three, the same warrior.

1-chronicles-18:12:8.summary: Abishai offers to strike Saul, showing the same man's warlike zeal.

1-chronicles-18:12:9.summary: Abishai son of Zeruiah kills a foreigner to save David.

1-chronicles-18:12:10.summary: Joab and Abishai his brother avenge Asahel, the same Abishai.
1-chronicles-18:12:10.why: Abishai's role in the Abner affair.

1-chronicles-18:12:11.summary: David sends Abishai to pursue Sheba, the same commander.

1-chronicles-18:13:3.summary: The Lord guards from all evil, a general protection theme.

1-chronicles-18:13:5.summary: God “gives salvation to kings” and “redeems David His servant,” matching the Lord saving David.

1-chronicles-19:3:5.summary: Israelite watchers scouting Bethel, a general spying parallel.

1-chronicles-19:3:7.summary: Love's qualities have no specific link to Ammon's suspicion of David.
